topics.title: Psychology: the word, the definition and its levels

learn.hook: Why does a batter freeze in a Super Over, why do friends fight over a group chat, why does a whole office turn quiet after a new boss arrives? One discipline asks all three questions: psychology.
points: Word origin: Greek 'psyche' (soul) + 'logos' (study or science). Early on, psychology meant 'the study of the soul'; today it is an empirical science.
Formal definition: psychology is the scientific study of mental processes, experiences and behaviour in different contexts.
Its three subject-matter pillars are mental processes (what the mind does), experiences (what we subjectively feel) and behaviour (how we respond).
Psychologists study people at several levels: the individual, the dyad (two people, e.g. mother-child), the group (e.g. a team) and the organisation (e.g. a company or hospital).
Because behaviour always happens somewhere, psychology studies it in its context: home, school, workplace, culture.

example.q: A researcher studies how a coach and a single bowler communicate, and a second researcher studies the work culture of an entire airline. At what levels are they working?
steps: Coach + one bowler = two people interacting.
A two-person unit is a dyad.
An entire airline is a formal structure of many groups.
That is the organisational level.
example.answer: First: dyadic level. Second: organisational level.

learn.reallife: When the Indian Railways studies why loco pilots get drowsy on night runs (individual), how a driver and co-driver coordinate (dyad), and how a whole zone's safety culture works (organisation), it is using psychology at every level.

quiz.q: Which is the most complete definition of psychology?
options: The study of mental illness and its cure
The scientific study of mental processes, experiences and behaviour in different contexts
The study of the brain and nervous system
quiz.explain: The modern definition includes mental processes, experiences and behaviour, studied scientifically and in context.
quiz.mistake: Picks the historical meaning or a single branch instead of the full definition

quiz.q: The word 'psychology' comes from two Greek words. What do they mean?
quiz.explain: 'Psyche' = soul, 'logos' = study or science.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the modern meaning instead of the Greek roots

quiz.q: A study of how two business partners resolve disagreements is at which level of analysis?
quiz.explain: Two people interacting form a dyad.
quiz.mistake: Treats any work-related study as organisational

quiz.q: Why is 'in different contexts' included in the definition of psychology?
options: Because psychologists only work in laboratories
Because behaviour is the same everywhere
Because behaviour and mental processes are shaped by the settings and cultures in which they occur
Because context is only important in history
quiz.explain: The same person may act differently at home, at school or at work, so context matters.
quiz.mistake: Assumes behaviour is fixed regardless of setting

quiz.q: A psychologist studies the morale of all employees in a large hospital. Which level is this?
quiz.explain: An entire institution with many groups is the organisational level.
quiz.mistake: Focuses on one employee rather than the whole institution

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the subject matter in the definition of psychology?
quiz.explain: Planetary motion is studied in physics; psychology deals with mind, experience and behaviour.
quiz.mistake: Thinks psychology covers all natural phenomena

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Modern psychology is no longer described simply as the 'study of the soul'. Reason (R): The soul cannot be observed or measured scientifically, so psychology shifted to studying mental processes, experiences and behaviour.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and the shift happened because psychology adopted scientific, observable subject matter.
quiz.mistake: Fails to see why the definition changed

quiz.q: Case: Neha, a psychologist, studies how a class of 40 students cooperates during a science fair. She is working at the
options: organisational level of a whole school system
quiz.explain: A class working together is a group.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a group with an entire organisation

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'Psychology... is that just mind-reading? What does it really study?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Mental processes, experiences and behaviour, studied scientifically. No mind-reading needed!
teach.nudge: You've told me some of it. Does psychology also study what we do, and is it scientific?

learn.hook: Your heart thumps as the Class 11 result link loads. Nobody else can see your heart rate, but it is behaviour too. Psychology counts the hidden reactions as well as the visible ones.
points: Mental processes are activities of the mind: remembering, learning, knowing, perceiving, feeling and thinking. They are not visible but are inferred.
Experiences are subjective: they are embedded in our awareness or consciousness, so they are known mainly through the person's own report.
Behaviour = responses or reactions to stimuli. Overt behaviour can be observed (running, smiling); covert behaviour is internal (heart rate rising, muscle tension).
Stimulus (S) and response (R) are the basic units: a stimulus is any change in the environment or body that evokes a response.
Psychology combines reflection on one's own experience with a scientific, objective approach to studying others.

example.q: Classify: (a) Arjun solves an algebra problem in his head; (b) Arjun's palms sweat before a speech; (c) Arjun waves to a friend.
steps: (a) Solving in the head is thinking, a mental process.
(b) Sweating palms are internal bodily responses, covert behaviour.
(c) Waving can be seen by others, overt behaviour.
example.answer: (a) mental process, (b) covert behaviour, (c) overt behaviour

learn.reallife: A cricket fan watching an India-Pakistan final: the roar is overt behaviour, the racing pulse is covert behaviour, the tension felt is an experience, and predicting the next ball is a mental process.

options: Increase in heart rate while waiting for exam results
quiz.explain: Covert responses are internal and not directly visible, like a rise in heart rate.

quiz.q: Why can't mental processes such as thinking be observed directly?
options: Because they happen only in children
Because they are internal activities of the mind and must be inferred from behaviour
quiz.explain: Mental processes are private; psychologists infer them from responses like answers or reaction times.

quiz.q: A dancer describes the deep joy she feels while performing. Psychology would call this joy her
quiz.explain: Subjective feelings in awareness are experiences.
quiz.mistake: Labels the feeling as the visible performance

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Psychologists study a person's experiences mainly through self-reports. Reason (R): Experiences are subjective and embedded in the person's awareness.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Since experiences are private to the experiencer, reports are the main window into them.
quiz.mistake: Doesn't connect subjectivity to the use of self-reports

quiz.q: Psychology is said to use both self-reflection and an objective approach. What does the objective approach mainly add?
options: Systematic, verifiable study of behaviour and mental processes
quiz.explain: The objective approach uses systematic methods so findings can be checked by others.
quiz.mistake: Thinks psychology is just personal reflection

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'If I can't see your thoughts, how can they be part of psychology? Explain the three things psychology studies!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Thoughts are mental processes, feelings are experiences, and behaviour can be overt or covert. Got it!
teach.nudge: Nice start! Can behaviour be hidden inside the body too? What do we call that?

learn.hook: An AIIMS research team guesses that sleeping less than five hours worsens memory. They don't just argue about it; they test it. That move from guess to test is what makes psychology a science.
points: Psychology has its roots in philosophy, but modern psychology grew by borrowing the methods of physics and biology.
Hypothetico-deductive model: start from a theory, deduce a testable hypothesis, test it through experiments or observation, then accept, revise or reject the theory.
Descartes' ideas about mind and body, and the biological sciences, shaped early psychology; evolutionary psychology explains behaviours in terms of how they helped our ancestors adapt and survive.
To be scientific, concepts must be objectively defined, measured precisely and studied so that other researchers can replicate (repeat) the findings.

example.q: Theory: practice strengthens memory. Write a hypothesis and say what would happen next in the hypothetico-deductive model.
steps: From the theory, deduce a specific prediction: students who revise a word list three times will recall more words than students who revise it once.
Test it with an experiment comparing the two groups.
If results support it, the theory gains support; if not, it is revised.
example.answer: Hypothesis: 'Three revisions lead to higher recall than one revision.' Next step: test it, then accept or revise the theory.

learn.reallife: ISRO engineers won't launch until a design has been tested and the test repeated. Psychology follows the same logic: a finding about, say, pilot fatigue is trusted only after it is measured objectively and replicated.

games.title: Hypothetico-deductive cycle
games.prompt: Arrange the steps of the hypothetico-deductive model

games.title: Science or not?
items: Modern psychology borrowed methods from physics and biology.
This is why it is treated as a natural science.
A scientific finding should be replicable by other researchers.
Replication is a core check in science.
Evolutionary psychology explains behaviour in terms of its adaptive value.
It asks how a behaviour helped survival and reproduction.
In science, a hypothesis that fails a test is always kept unchanged.
The theory is revised or rejected if evidence contradicts it.
Psychology has no connection at all with philosophy.
Its roots lie in philosophy.

quiz.q: In the hypothetico-deductive model, a hypothesis is
options: a testable prediction derived from a theory
a personal opinion that cannot be tested
a summary written after all research is over
quiz.explain: A hypothesis is deduced from theory and then tested.
quiz.mistake: Treats a hypothesis as already proven

quiz.q: Which feature most clearly makes psychology a natural science?
options: Objective definitions, measurement and replicable experiments
quiz.explain: Scientific status comes from objective, measurable, replicable methods.
quiz.mistake: Thinks studying animals alone makes it a natural science

quiz.q: Evolutionary psychology would most likely explain fear of snakes as
options: a behaviour that helped ancestors survive
quiz.explain: It looks for the adaptive, survival value of behaviour.

quiz.q: Which philosopher's ideas on mind and body are linked with the early natural-science approach to psychology?
quiz.explain: Descartes' ideas about mind-body interaction influenced psychology's natural-science roots.
quiz.mistake: Picks a thinker from a different field

quiz.q: A study's result could not be repeated when three other labs tried it. What scientific requirement is missing?
quiz.explain: Findings must be replicable to be trusted.
quiz.mistake: Doesn't recognise replication as a criterion

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Psychology is considered a natural science. Reason (R): Psychology has its roots in philosophy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but roots in philosophy do not explain its natural-science status; scientific methods do.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any true reason must explain the assertion

quiz.q: Why must a concept like 'anxiety' be defined objectively before research?
options: So that no data are needed
So it can be measured in the same way by different researchers
quiz.explain: Objective definitions allow precise measurement and replication.

quiz.q: What happens to a theory in the hypothetico-deductive model when tests repeatedly contradict its hypothesis?
options: It is ignored and kept as it is
quiz.explain: Evidence against a hypothesis leads to revising or rejecting the theory.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can psychology be a science like physics? It's about feelings!'
teach.praise: Cheep! Theory, hypothesis, testing, objective measurement and replication. Feelings can be studied scientifically!
teach.nudge: You mentioned science, but how do psychologists actually check their ideas?

learn.hook: Two families face the same job loss after a factory closes. One falls apart; the other pulls through by leaning on neighbours, relatives and a self-help group. Biology alone can't explain the difference; society and culture can.
points: Humans are social beings, so psychology studies behaviour in its socio-cultural context: family, community, school, workplace and the wider culture.
The same event can be explained through social and cultural factors, e.g. a poor family's resilience may come from strong social support and shared beliefs.
As a social science, psychology focuses on how people relate to each other and to the wider society.
Psychology is both a natural science (biological, objective methods) and a social science (socio-cultural context), so it acts as a bridge between them.

example.q: Explain with one example why psychology is called both a natural and a social science.
steps: Natural science side: stress raises heart rate and stress hormones, which can be measured objectively.
Social science side: how much stress a person feels after losing a job depends on family support, community and culture.
Psychology studies both together.
example.answer: Stress has measurable biological effects (natural science) and is shaped by social support and culture (social science).

learn.reallife: During the Kerala floods of 2018, communities organised rescue and relief through fishermen, volunteers and local groups. Understanding how people coped needs both the biology of stress and the social science of community support.

quiz.q: What would a purely biological explanation miss when explaining how people cope after a disaster?

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'If psychology is a science, why does it care about society and culture?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Psychology is a bridge: natural science and social science together.
teach.nudge: Good! But is psychology only one kind of science, or both?

learn.hook: Picture a fMRI scanner at a Delhi hospital. A volunteer imagines kicking a football and a region of her brain lights up, though she hasn't moved. Thought shows up in brain activity, yet thought is not the same thing as the brain.
points: The mind is not a physical structure like the brain, but it depends on the brain; mind and brain are related but not identical.
Brain imaging such as fMRI (functional magnetic resonance imaging) shows that mental activities are accompanied by changes in brain activity.
The mind can influence the body: positive visualisation and optimism are linked with better recovery, and psychoneuroimmunology studies how the mind affects the immune system.
Behaviour is a response to internal (e.g. hunger) or external (e.g. a loud horn) stimuli; it can be simple or complex, short-lived or enduring.

example.q: Sameer, recovering from surgery, practises imagining himself walking and healing each day, and his doctor notes faster recovery than expected. Which idea does this illustrate?
steps: He is using positive visualisation, a mental activity.
Better recovery is a bodily outcome.
So a mental activity is influencing the body.
example.answer: The mind can influence the body (mind-body relationship; studied in psychoneuroimmunology).

learn.reallife: Hospitals like AIIMS now include psychologists in teams for heart patients and cancer care, because worry, hope and stress measurably affect immunity and recovery.

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Is the mind just the brain? Can my thoughts change my body?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Mind isn't a physical structure, it depends on the brain, and it can affect the body. Mind blown!
teach.nudge: Close! Is the mind the same as the brain, and can it affect the body?

learn.hook: 'Birds of a feather flock together.' Also: 'Opposites attract.' Your nani can quote both with full confidence. Which one is true? Common sense can't settle it; research can.
points: Everyone acts as a lay (everyday) psychologist, explaining behaviour from common sense and experience.
Common-sense explanations are often based on hindsight: they explain an event after it happens but rarely predict it.
Common sense is frequently contradictory, e.g. 'Birds of a feather flock together' vs 'Opposites attract'.
Scientific psychology tests common-sense beliefs systematically; sometimes evidence supports them and sometimes contradicts them.
Example of research contradicting popular belief: praising children for effort, rather than for being 'smart', makes them more willing to take on hard tasks.

example.q: Your friend says, 'Of course India won; the team was confident.' Had India lost he would have said, 'They were overconfident.' What problem with common sense does this show, and how would a psychologist test the claim?
steps: He explains the outcome only after it happens: hindsight.
Either outcome can be 'explained', so the explanation predicts nothing.
A psychologist would define 'confidence', measure it before matches and check whether it predicts results.
example.answer: Hindsight; test by measuring confidence beforehand and checking if it predicts performance.

learn.reallife: Before banking apps launch new features, Indian fintech startups run A/B tests instead of trusting gut feeling, because users often behave differently from what 'common sense' predicts.

topics.title: Early schools: Wundt, structuralism, functionalism, Gestalt

learn.hook: 1879, Leipzig, Germany: a professor sets up a room with metronomes and timers to study conscious experience. That room, Wilhelm Wundt's laboratory, is usually counted as the birthplace of modern psychology.
points: Wilhelm Wundt set up the first experimental psychology laboratory at Leipzig, Germany, in 1879.

Structuralism (Wundt; carried to the USA by Titchener) studied the structure of the mind, breaking conscious experience into elements using introspection, i.e. trained observers reporting their own mental processes.
Functionalism (William James, John Dewey) asked what the mind does and how behaviour helps people adapt to their environment. James published 'Principles of Psychology' in 1890.
Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Kohler, Kurt Koffka; around 1912) held that we perceive organised wholes, not separate elements: the whole differs from the sum of its parts.
Landmarks: 1879 Wundt's lab; 1890 James's 'Principles'; 1900 Freud's 'Interpretation of Dreams'; 1905 Binet-Simon intelligence test; 1912 Gestalt school.

example.q: A researcher asks a trained observer to describe the sensations and images that make up the experience of tasting a mango. Which school does this belong to and why?
steps: The observer reports his own conscious experience: introspection.
The goal is to break experience into its elements.
Introspection to find elements of consciousness is the method of structuralism.
example.answer: Structuralism (Wundt/Titchener) using introspection

learn.reallife: A Bollywood song isn't heard as separate notes but as one melody; a cricket field's 11 fielders are seen as a 'field setting'. The Gestalt school built its whole approach on this whole-before-parts experience.

topics.title: Later perspectives: behaviourism to the cognitive view

learn.hook: One psychologist says, 'Forget the mind, show me behaviour.' Another says, 'Behaviour hides unconscious wishes.' A third says, 'People choose to grow.' Same species, very different lenses.
points: Behaviourism (John Watson, around 1910s; later B.F. Skinner): psychology should study only observable, measurable behaviour, explained as stimulus-response (S-R) links; the mind was set aside.
Psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud): behaviour is driven by unconscious desires and conflicts; developed as a way to understand and treat psychological disorders.

Humanistic perspective (Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow): humans have free will and a natural drive to grow and self-actualise (realise their potential); it criticised the mechanistic view of behaviourism and the pessimism of psychoanalysis.
Cognitive perspective: the mind is like an information processor (as in a computer) that takes in, stores and uses information.

Constructivism within the cognitive view: people actively construct their understanding of the world (Jean Piaget); Lev Vygotsky stressed that this construction happens through social and cultural interaction.

example.q: Which perspective fits each statement? (a) 'Rewards shape a child's habits.' (b) 'A slip of the tongue may reveal a hidden wish.' (c) 'Every person strives to fulfil their potential.'
steps: (a) Behaviour shaped by consequences, observable: behaviourism.
(b) Hidden wish = unconscious: psychoanalysis.
(c) Striving to fulfil potential = self-actualisation: humanistic.
example.answer: (a) Behaviourism, (b) Psychoanalysis, (c) Humanistic

learn.reallife: A food-delivery app sends you a reward badge for every fifth order (behaviourist), while its design team studies how you search and remember menus (cognitive). Modern products quietly mix perspectives.

learn.hook: Long before Leipzig, Indian thinkers debated the nature of consciousness, the self and the mind-body relationship. Modern lab psychology in India, though, began at a university in Calcutta in 1915.
points: Indian philosophical traditions contain rich ideas on consciousness, the self, the mind-body relationship and mental functions.

1915: Calcutta University introduced the first syllabus of experimental psychology and set up India's first psychology laboratory (N.N. Sengupta played a key role); in 1916 it started India's first Department of Psychology.
Girindra Shekhar Bose, trained in psychoanalysis, founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Association in 1922.
Departments later started at Mysore, Patna and other universities; Durganand Sinha traced the growth of modern Indian psychology in four phases, the later one stressing indigenisation.
Indigenisation: making psychological theory and research culturally relevant to Indian society instead of copying Western models uncritically.

example.q: Put these in order: Bose founds the Indian Psychoanalytical Association; Wundt's lab; Calcutta University sets up India's first psychology laboratory.
steps: Wundt's lab: 1879.
Calcutta laboratory: 1915.
Indian Psychoanalytical Association: 1922.
example.answer: Wundt (1879) → Calcutta (1915) → Indian Psychoanalytical Association (1922)

learn.reallife: Today Tele-MANAS, India's mental-health helpline (14416), and research in IITs and universities on stress in farmers, students and soldiers show psychology working on problems that matter in Indian society: indigenisation in action.

topics.title: Branches I: cognitive, biological, developmental, social, cultural

learn.hook: A toddler's first words, a stroke patient's memory loss, a crowd's panic at a railway station, and why some cultures greet with a namaste and others with a handshake: each belongs to a different branch of psychology.
points: Cognitive psychology: attention, memory, perception, learning, problem solving, decision making and language.
Biological psychology studies brain-behaviour links; neuropsychology examines how brain damage or brain processes relate to behaviour and mental functions.
Developmental psychology: physical, cognitive and socio-emotional changes across the life span, from conception to old age.
Social psychology: how other people (real or imagined) influence our thoughts, feelings and behaviour, e.g. attitudes, conformity, prejudice.
Cross-cultural and cultural psychology: the role of culture in shaping behaviour and how behaviour differs across cultures.

example.q: Match each research question to its branch: (a) How does a 70-year-old's memory differ from a 20-year-old's? (b) Does injury to the frontal lobe affect planning? (c) Why do people conform to group opinion?
steps: (a) Change with age = developmental (memory = cognitive also, but the focus is age).
(b) Brain injury and behaviour = neuropsychology/biological.
(c) Influence of others = social.
example.answer: (a) Developmental, (b) Biological/neuropsychology, (c) Social

learn.reallife: When the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru, assesses memory after a head injury, it draws on neuropsychology; when an ad agency studies peer influence on teens, it draws on social psychology.

topics.title: Branches II: environmental, health, clinical, I/O, educational

learn.hook: Why does a crowded local train feel more stressful on a hot day? Why do some patients skip their medicines? Why do some employees thrive under one manager and quit under another? Psychology has a branch for each.
points: Environmental psychology: how the physical environment (noise, heat, crowding, pollution, design) and behaviour affect each other, including pro-environment behaviour.
Health psychology: psychological factors (stress, lifestyle, coping) in health and illness and in staying healthy.

Clinical and counselling psychology: causes, diagnosis and treatment of psychological problems; counselling also helps people with everyday adjustment and career choices. They differ from psychiatrists, who are medically trained and can prescribe medicines.
Industrial/organisational (I/O) psychology: workplace behaviour such as selection, training, motivation, leadership and job satisfaction.
Educational psychology: how people learn and how teaching can be improved; school psychology applies this in schools, e.g. identifying learning difficulties.

example.q: Which branch? (a) A Mumbai firm asks how open offices affect concentration. (b) A heart patient is helped to stop smoking. (c) A school identifies a child with reading difficulties.
steps: (a) Physical design and behaviour = environmental (also I/O, but the focus is the physical space).
(b) Lifestyle and illness = health psychology.
(c) Learning difficulties in school = educational/school psychology.
example.answer: (a) Environmental, (b) Health, (c) Educational/school

learn.reallife: Swachh Bharat campaigns used psychological insights on habits and social norms to change sanitation behaviour, a classic case of environmental and health psychology at national scale.

topics.title: Specialised fields and psychology's links with other disciplines

learn.hook: Why do Nobel prizes in economics sometimes go to psychologists? Herbert Simon (1978) and Daniel Kahneman (2002) showed that real people don't decide like perfect calculators. Psychology leaks into every field.
points: Specialised fields: sports psychology (performance, motivation of athletes), forensic psychology (law and crime, witness testimony), military, aviation and space psychology (selection, stress, isolation), psycholinguistics (language acquisition and use), community psychology (community-level problems and wellbeing).

Psychology is interdisciplinary: it shares questions with philosophy (mind, knowledge), medicine (health, illness), economics (decision making, consumer behaviour), political science (power, voting) and sociology (socialisation, groups).

It also links with computer science (artificial intelligence, models of thinking), law and criminology (eyewitnesses, criminal behaviour), mass communication (effects of media), music and fine arts (emotion, creativity), and architecture and engineering (designing spaces and machines for human use).
Exam tip: to match a problem with a branch, ask 'What is the main psychological question here?', not just 'Where does it happen?'

example.q: An Indian shooter's scores drop sharply in finals. A psychologist trains her in relaxation and focus routines. Which branch, and which neighbouring discipline is involved?
steps: The main question is athletic performance under pressure.

It overlaps with medicine and physiology (sports science).
example.answer: Sports psychology (linked with medicine/sports science)

learn.hook: You don't need a lab coat to use psychology. Spacing out revision, calming yourself before a viva, or understanding why a friend is upset: that's psychology on a weekday afternoon.
points: Psychological knowledge helps solve personal problems (stress, relationships, decisions) and social problems (health, conflict, environment).
Self-understanding: knowing your own strengths, emotions and habits helps you make better decisions, e.g. adopting effective study habits like planned schedules, short breaks and active recall.
Psychology contributes to social issues: promoting health behaviour, protecting the environment, reducing prejudice and supporting social justice.
When distress becomes hard to manage, talking to a trusted adult or a professional helps; in India, Tele-MANAS (14416) offers free mental-health support.

example.answer: Spread study over days with short breaks, and test yourself (active recall) instead of re-reading.

learn.hook: A school counsellor notices that some students go silent in class. Before she can help, she has to know what exactly is happening, when it will happen, and why. Those are the first three goals of psychological research.
points: Psychologists use systematic, scientific methods because casual observation and opinion can be biased and unreliable.
The four goals of psychological enquiry: description, prediction, explanation, and control (with application of findings).
Description: defining a behaviour precisely and measuring it, so it can be distinguished from other behaviours (e.g. defining 'study habits' as hours studied, place, method).
Prediction: once relationships between behaviours are known, a behaviour can be forecast with some accuracy (e.g. more practice → better performance). Predictions are probabilistic, not certain.
Explanation: identifying the causes or antecedents (conditions that come before) that lead to a behaviour.

example.q: A researcher records that students who sleep less than six hours score lower on tests, then expects next year's sleepy students to score lower, and finally finds that sleep loss weakens attention. Identify the goal at each step.
steps: Recording what happens = description.
Expecting the same relationship next year = prediction.
Finding the cause (weak attention due to sleep loss) = explanation.
example.answer: Description → prediction → explanation

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' safety cells first describe driver errors, then predict which shifts are risky, then explain the causes (fatigue), before designing rosters to control the problem: all four goals in one system.

teach.nudge: Nice! You've got some goals. What about predicting or explaining behaviour?

topics.title: Control, application and the steps of research

learn.hook: Knowing that screen time before bed hurts sleep is useful. Designing a hostel rule that actually improves sleep is the payoff. That's the goal of control, and research reaches it through four clear steps.
points: Control: making a behaviour happen, reducing it or increasing it; it leads to application, i.e. using findings to improve lives (e.g. therapy, training programmes).
Step 1, conceptualising a problem: choose a topic and form a testable hypothesis (a tentative answer).
Step 2, collecting data: decide the participants, the method (observation, experiment, survey…), the tools (tests, questionnaires) and the procedure.
Step 3, drawing conclusions: analyse data with statistical methods and graphs to see whether the hypothesis is supported.
Step 4, revising research conclusions: confirm or modify the theory; new questions arise, so research is cyclic.

example.q: Hypothesis: 'Students who take a 10-minute walk before an exam feel less anxious.' Outline what happens in each of the four research steps.
steps: Conceptualising: topic = exam anxiety; hypothesis stated above.
Collecting data: choose Class 11 students, randomly give some a walk, measure anxiety with a questionnaire.
Drawing conclusions: compare average anxiety scores using statistics and graphs.
Revising: if supported, the theory on exercise and anxiety is confirmed; new questions follow (how long a walk?).
example.answer: Conceptualise → collect data → draw conclusions → revise conclusions (and the cycle continues).

learn.reallife: Kota coaching centres introducing counselling and sleep schedules after studies on student stress show control/application: research findings turned into interventions.

topics.title: Research paradigms and the nature of psychological data

learn.hook: Two researchers study farmers after a failed monsoon. One counts days of lost sleep; the other sits with farmers and listens to what loss means to them. Both are doing psychology, using different paradigms.
points: Scientific (positivist) paradigm: aims at objective measurement, testing hypotheses and finding general cause-effect laws.
Interpretive paradigm: aims at understanding people's subjective experiences and the meanings they attach to them, in their own context.
Psychological data are not independent of context: the participant's characteristics (age, gender, background) and the setting influence responses.

Types of data: demographic (age, gender, education, income), physical (housing, room size, facilities), physiological (heart rate, blood pressure, pupil dilation) and psychological (intelligence, personality, emotions, values).
Psychological data are not direct measures: intelligence or anxiety is inferred from responses on tests, interviews or behaviour.

example.q: Classify: (a) family income, (b) blood pressure, (c) creativity score, (d) number of rooms at home.
steps: (a) Income is a background characteristic = demographic.
(b) Blood pressure is a bodily measure = physiological.
(c) Creativity is a mental attribute = psychological.
(d) Rooms describe living conditions = physical.
example.answer: (a) demographic, (b) physiological, (c) psychological, (d) physical

learn.reallife: A Census-style survey records demographic data, an Apollo hospital stress study records heart rate (physiological), and a startup's employee survey measures motivation (psychological). Together they give a full picture.

learn.hook: Sit at a busy Chennai bus stop for an hour and note who gives up a seat to whom. You've just collected observational data, but only if you decided in advance what to watch and how to record it.
points: Observation is a systematic, organised and selective process with three steps: selection (what to observe), recording (notes, tallies, video) and analysis of the data.
Naturalistic observation is done in real-life settings without manipulation; controlled observation happens in a structured setting such as a lab.
Non-participant observation: the observer stays apart and observes without becoming part of the group (sometimes using one-way mirrors or cameras).
Participant observation: the observer becomes part of the group being studied, which gives insider understanding but takes time to build acceptance.
Strengths: rich data about natural behaviour; weaknesses: time-consuming, labour-intensive and prone to observer bias (seeing what one expects).

example.q: Design a simple observation to study sharing among Class 2 children during lunch.
steps: Selection: decide the behaviour to observe, e.g. offering food to another child.
Recording: use a tally sheet with 5-minute slots for 3 days.
Choose type: naturalistic, non-participant, observing from a corner.
Analysis: count sharing acts per child and compare boys/girls or ages.
example.answer: A naturalistic, non-participant observation with a tally sheet and clear definition of 'sharing'.

learn.reallife: Anthropologists and psychologists studying fishing communities on the Kerala coast often live with them for months as participant observers, learning about cooperation that a questionnaire could never capture.

learn.hook: Does background music help or hurt memorising? Observation can't tell you, because too many things vary at once. An experiment changes one thing on purpose and watches what happens.
points: Experiments establish cause-and-effect relationships by manipulating one variable under controlled conditions.
Independent variable (IV): the variable the experimenter manipulates (the cause). Dependent variable (DV): the behaviour measured as the effect.
Operational definition: defining a variable by how it is measured or manipulated, e.g. 'memory = number of words recalled out of 20'.
Experimental group receives the IV (treatment); the control group does not and serves as the baseline for comparison. Both should be treated the same in all other ways.

example.q: Students learn 20 words: Group A with loud music, Group B in silence. Recall is then tested. Identify IV, DV, experimental and control groups.
steps: What is changed on purpose? Presence of music → IV.
What is measured? Number of words recalled → DV.
Group A gets the treatment (music) → experimental group.
Group B gets no music → control group.
example.answer: IV = music; DV = words recalled; Group A = experimental; Group B = control

learn.reallife: Before a new Hindi-reading app is rolled out in government schools, a pilot can compare classes using the app (experimental) with similar classes that don't (control): the app is the IV, reading scores the DV.

topics.title: Controlling extraneous variables; types and limits of experiments

learn.hook: You find that students who used a new revision app scored higher. But what if the app group also happened to be the brighter section, or took the test in a quieter room? Those sneaky other factors can ruin an experiment.
points: Extraneous (confounding) variables: variables other than the IV that may influence the DV, e.g. participants' intelligence, room noise, time of day, order of tasks. They must be controlled, or the result can't be blamed on the IV.

Control techniques: elimination (remove the variable, e.g. soundproof room); constancy of conditions (keep it the same for all, e.g. same time and instructions); counterbalancing (vary task order so order/sequence effects cancel out, e.g. half do A then B, half B then A); random assignment (every participant has an equal chance of being in any group).
Laboratory experiment: maximum control but artificial setting. Field experiment: done in a natural setting (school, factory); more realistic, less control.
Quasi-experiment: the IV is selected rather than manipulated and groups are not randomly formed, e.g. comparing children who lived through an earthquake with those who did not.
Limitations: artificiality, ethical limits on what can be manipulated, and difficulty in controlling every extraneous variable.

example.q: Every participant solves puzzle A and then puzzle B. Scores on B are higher. Why might this be misleading, and how would you fix it?
steps: B always comes second, so practice or fatigue (sequence effect) may explain the difference.
Fix: counterbalance. Half the participants do A then B, the other half B then A.
Order effects now cancel out across the two halves.
example.answer: Sequence effect; control it by counterbalancing (AB for half, BA for the other half).

learn.reallife: Studying how the 2001 Gujarat earthquake affected children's later anxiety can only be done as a quasi-experiment: no researcher can (or should) create an earthquake.

learn.hook: In some cities, ice-cream sales and drowning cases rise together. Does ice cream cause drowning? No: summer heat drives both. Correlation tells you that two things move together, not why.
points: Correlational research studies the relationship between two variables to see whether, and how strongly, they vary together, so that one can be predicted from the other.
The correlation coefficient (r) ranges from -1.0 to +1.0. Its sign shows direction; its size (closeness to 1, ignoring sign) shows strength.

Positive correlation: both increase together (study hours and marks). Negative correlation: one increases as the other decreases (hours of TV and marks). Zero correlation: no relationship (shoe size and honesty).
Correlation does not imply causation: a third variable may cause both, or the direction of cause may be unknown.
Correlation is useful when variables cannot be manipulated ethically or practically, e.g. smoking and health.

example.q: Which shows the strongest relationship: r = +0.45, r = -0.82, r = +0.10?
steps: Strength depends on how close r is to 1, ignoring the sign.
0.82 is the largest, so -0.82 is strongest (a strong negative correlation).

learn.reallife: Market analysts on Dalal Street note that some stock prices move together (positive correlation) and some move opposite (negative), but they never assume one stock causes another to rise.

learn.hook: Before elections, TV channels ask thousands of voters what they think. Before launching a new snack, companies ask what people like. Survey research is how psychology hears from many people quickly.
points: Surveys collect information about people's opinions, attitudes, beliefs and behaviour, often from a large population, usually through interviews, questionnaires or telephone.
An interview is a purposeful conversation: the interviewer asks questions, the interviewee answers.

Structured (standardised) interview: fixed questions asked in a fixed order, often with fixed response options; easy to compare. Unstructured interview: flexible questions that can be changed according to the answers; gives depth.
Interview formats: individual to individual, individual to group, group to individual (e.g. a selection board), and group to group.

example.q: A five-member UPSC-style interview board questions one candidate. Which interview format is this, and is it likely to be structured or unstructured?
steps: Several interviewers, one interviewee → group to individual.
Board members may follow up on the candidate's answers flexibly.
So it often has unstructured elements, though some boards use standard questions.
example.answer: Group-to-individual interview, usually semi-flexible (unstructured elements).

learn.reallife: The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) uses trained interviewers with standardised questions across all states so that answers from Assam and Gujarat can be compared fairly.

topics.title: Questionnaires, telephone surveys and survey problems

learn.hook: 'Do you ever litter?' Almost everyone ticks 'No'. Yet the streets tell another story. Surveys are powerful, but people don't always report what they really do.
points: Questionnaire survey: a printed or online set of questions. Open-ended questions let people answer freely; closed-ended questions give fixed choices: yes/no, multiple choice or a rating scale (e.g. 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree).
Mailed questionnaires reach many people cheaply but often have a low return rate.
Telephone survey: quick and inexpensive; but people may be uncooperative or hang up, and the interviewer cannot see non-verbal cues.

Problems of surveys: social desirability (giving answers that look good), faking, and inaccurate recall (people forget or misremember past behaviour); people may also not reveal what they really think.

example.q: Write one open-ended and one closed-ended (rating-scale) question on study stress.
steps: Open-ended: let the student answer in their own words.
'What makes studying stressful for you?'
Closed-ended rating scale: 'I feel stressed while studying.' 1 (never) to 5 (always).
example.answer: Open: 'What makes studying stressful for you?' Closed: 'I feel stressed while studying: 1 never - 5 always.'

learn.reallife: Online customer-feedback forms after a Swiggy or IRCTC booking use star ratings (closed-ended) plus an optional comment box (open-ended), combining easy scoring with rich detail.

topics.title: Psychological tests: reliability, validity and norms

learn.hook: A weighing scale that shows 52 kg, then 47 kg, then 58 kg in one minute is useless. A psychological test is no different: if it isn't consistent and accurate, its scores mean nothing.
points: Psychological tests are standardised, objective instruments that measure individual differences in abilities, aptitude, interests, personality, values and so on.
A standardised test must have reliability, validity and norms, and a standard procedure for administration and scoring.

Reliability = consistency of scores. Test-retest reliability: the same test given to the same people at two times; the correlation shows temporal stability. Split-half reliability: scores on two equivalent halves of the test (e.g. odd vs even items) are correlated to check internal consistency.
Validity: the test measures what it claims to measure (an anxiety test should measure anxiety, not reading ability).
Norms: the average or normal performance of a large, representative group, used to interpret an individual's score.

example.q: A new aptitude test gives students similar scores in May and again in July. Separately, the scores don't predict how well they do in the related course. Comment on reliability and validity.
steps: Similar scores over two months → good test-retest reliability (consistent).
Not predicting course performance → poor validity (it may not measure aptitude).
A test can be reliable without being valid.
example.answer: Reliable (test-retest) but low in validity.

learn.reallife: Before a recruitment test is used by public-sector banks, it must be standardised on a large Indian sample (norms), give stable scores (reliability) and actually predict job performance (validity).

topics.title: Kinds of tests and the case study

learn.hook: A child in a remote hamlet who can't yet read may look 'weak' on a written test, but shine on a puzzle with blocks. The type of test you pick can decide what you find.
points: By language: verbal tests need literacy (reading/writing in a language); non-verbal tests use symbols, figures or pictures; performance tests require manipulating objects (e.g. arranging blocks), so language is minimal.
By administration: individual tests are given to one person at a time (allow close observation); group tests are given to many at once (save time).
By time: speed tests have a strict time limit and items of similar difficulty; power tests have no strict time limit and items arranged in increasing order of difficulty.
Case study: an in-depth study of a single person or small unit (family, group) using several methods: interviews, observation, questionnaires and tests.
Case studies are valuable in clinical settings and for rare phenomena, but their findings cannot be easily generalised to others. Choosing a method depends on the research question.

example.q: Choose a method: (a) Does a new drug reduce exam anxiety? (b) How does a rare memory disorder affect one patient's daily life? (c) What do 2,000 voters think of a policy?
steps: (a) Cause-effect → experiment.
(b) Rare, in-depth, one person → case study.
(c) Opinions of many → survey.
example.answer: (a) Experiment, (b) Case study, (c) Survey

learn.reallife: Recruitment rounds at Indian airlines use group aptitude tests first (efficient), then individual tests and interviews for shortlisted pilots (in-depth assessment).

learn.hook: '78% of students felt stressed' is one kind of answer. 'I feel like I'm carrying my whole family's dreams on my back' is another. Psychologists need both numbers and stories.
points: Quantitative method: data in numbers (scores, frequencies) analysed with statistics such as averages, percentages and correlations.
Qualitative method: data in words, narratives and descriptions (from interviews, diaries, field notes), analysed for themes and meanings.
The two methods are complementary: using both together (sometimes called triangulation) gives a fuller and more confident understanding.
A limitation of qualitative data is subjective interpretation: different researchers may read the same narrative differently.

example.q: A study on online classes during the pandemic collects (a) average hours of screen time and (b) students' written accounts of loneliness. Classify each and say why using both helps.
steps: (a) Numbers → quantitative.
(b) Written accounts → qualitative.
Numbers show the size of the problem; accounts explain how it felt and why.
example.answer: (a) quantitative, (b) qualitative; together they give a fuller picture.

learn.reallife: The Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) gives numbers on reading levels across India, while field studies record children's and teachers' own voices. Policymakers use both.

learn.hook: A thermometer reading of 0 °C doesn't mean 'no temperature', and an IQ of 0 doesn't mean 'no intelligence'. Psychological measurement has no true zero, which limits how we can compare scores.
points: Lack of a true zero point: psychological measures have no absolute zero (a score of 0 on an anxiety test doesn't mean zero anxiety), so we can't say one person has 'twice' another's ability.
Relative nature of psychological tools: tests developed in one culture (e.g. Western) may not suit another; they need cultural adaptation before use in India.
Subjective interpretation of qualitative data is a further limitation (see the previous topic).
Confidentiality: because psychological data are personal, researchers must keep them confidential and protect participants' privacy, e.g. using codes instead of names.

example.q: Rahul scores 40 and Priya scores 80 on a creativity test. Can we say Priya is 'twice as creative'? Why or why not?
steps: Ratio statements need a true zero point.
Psychological tests lack a true zero.
So we can only say Priya scored higher, not that she is twice as creative.
example.answer: No; without a true zero, only 'Priya scored higher' can be said.

learn.reallife: When Indian researchers use a personality test designed in the USA, they translate, adapt items (e.g. replacing 'baseball' with 'cricket') and build Indian norms, addressing the relative nature of tools.

learn.hook: Would you join a study if you didn't know what it involved, couldn't leave, and never heard what it found? Ethics rules exist so that the people who make research possible are never harmed by it.
points: Voluntary participation: people take part by their own free choice, without pressure, and can withdraw at any time.
Informed consent: before the study, participants are told what it involves (procedure, possible discomfort) and agree to take part. For children, consent is also taken from parents or guardians.
Debriefing: after the study, participants are given a full explanation of its purpose and any anxiety or discomfort caused is removed, so they leave in the same state as they came.
Sharing results: participants should be told the results of the study in a form they understand. Confidentiality of data must also be maintained.
Exam format: list voluntary participation, informed consent, debriefing, sharing results and confidentiality, and apply them to the study given.

example.q: A researcher plans to test how criticism affects Class 9 students' performance. List the ethical steps she must take.
steps: Ask schools, parents and students; students join freely and may withdraw (voluntary participation).
Explain the procedure beforehand and take consent from parents and assent from students (informed consent).
After the task, explain that the criticism was part of the study and reassure students (debriefing).
Keep data confidential and share the overall results with participants.
example.answer: Voluntary participation, informed consent, debriefing, confidentiality and sharing results.

learn.reallife: Clinical trials at Indian hospitals must be approved by an ethics committee and registered with the Clinical Trials Registry-India; patients sign informed-consent forms in their own language before taking part.

topics.title: Meaning of development: growth, maturation and development

learn.hook: Your baby cousin goes from lying flat to crawling to running around the wedding hall in barely two years. Your grandparents keep changing too, in wisdom, patience and health. Development never really stops.
points: Development is the pattern of progressive, orderly and predictable changes that begin at conception and continue throughout life, until death.

Growth: increase in the size of the body or its parts (height, weight). Maturation: changes that follow an orderly sequence largely set by the genetic plan (e.g. walking emerges when the body is ready).
Development is broader: it includes growth and maturation but also changes in thinking, emotions and social relationships brought about by experience.
Development involves three interacting processes: biological (physical changes), cognitive (thought, intelligence, language) and socio-emotional (emotions, personality, relationships).

example.q: Classify: (a) Arjun grows 6 cm taller in a year. (b) A baby starts walking at about the same age as most babies, whatever the training. (c) A teenager learns to manage anger and make friends.
steps: (a) Increase in size = growth.
(b) Change following a genetic timetable = maturation.
(c) Change in emotions and relationships through experience = socio-emotional development.
example.answer: (a) growth, (b) maturation, (c) development (socio-emotional)

learn.reallife: Anganwadi workers in the ICDS programme track a child's height and weight (growth), check milestones like sitting and walking (maturation) and support play and language (wider development).

teach.praise: Chirp! Growth is size, maturation follows the genes, development is the whole orderly change. I'm developing too!

learn.hook: A 75-year-old learning to use UPI to pay her vegetable vendor is still developing. The life-span view says no age is 'finished': we gain and lose abilities at every stage.
points: Development is lifelong: no single age period dominates; every stage from infancy to old age matters.
Development is multi-dimensional (biological, cognitive, socio-emotional) and multi-directional: some abilities increase while others decrease (e.g. older adults gain wisdom but may lose speed).
Development is highly plastic: abilities can be modified by experience at any age, e.g. memory can improve with training even in old age.
Development is influenced by historical conditions: those growing up during the Emergency, the 1991 reforms or the COVID-19 pandemic had different experiences.
Development is studied by many disciplines (psychology, sociology, biology, medicine…) and is contextual: it happens in a setting of heredity, environment, culture and family.

example.q: Teens who grew up with smartphones learnt online skills earlier than their parents did at the same age. Which principle of the life-span perspective does this illustrate?
steps: The difference is due to the time period in which they grew up.
Changes in society and technology over time shape development.
That is the influence of historical conditions.
example.answer: Development is influenced by historical conditions.

learn.reallife: Grandparents across India who learnt UPI payments and video calls during and after the pandemic show plasticity: learning new skills well into old age.

learn.hook: Two seeds of the same mango variety are planted, one in rich soil with water, the other in a dry patch. The genes are identical; the harvest isn't. Human development works much the same way.
points: Heredity: characteristics passed from parents to children through genes. Genotype = a person's genetic heritage (the genes); phenotype = the observable characteristics (height, eye colour, personality traits) that result.
Environment: the physical and social surroundings (nutrition, family, school, culture) in which a person develops.
Nature and nurture interact: development is the product of both, not of either alone.
Genes set a range within which a trait can develop; the environment determines where in that range a person ends up (e.g. a child with genes for tallness may stay short with poor nutrition).
Some traits (e.g. eye colour) are strongly shaped by genes; others (e.g. language spoken, values) are much more open to environmental influence.

example.q: Identical twins (same genes) are raised apart, one with good nutrition and schooling, the other with poor nutrition. As adults, the first is taller and scores higher on tests. Explain using genotype and phenotype.
steps: Same genes → same genotype.
Different environments → different observable outcomes (phenotype).
Genes set a possible range; the environment decided where each twin ended up within it.
example.answer: Same genotype, different phenotypes, because the environment works within the range genes allow.

learn.reallife: Poshan Abhiyaan's focus on the first 1,000 days of life recognises that even good genetic potential needs nutrition and care to be realised.

learn.hook: A child's school marks can drop because her father's factory shifted him to night shifts. She never set foot in that factory, yet it shaped her life. Bronfenbrenner's model explains how.
points: Urie Bronfenbrenner described the environment as five nested systems around the child.

Microsystem: the immediate settings the child directly interacts with (family, school, peers, neighbourhood). Mesosystem: relations between microsystems (e.g. parent-teacher meetings, family-peer links).
Exosystem: settings the child is not directly part of but which affect the child (e.g. a parent's workplace, local government decisions).
Macrosystem: the broader culture, values, customs and laws of the society.
Chronosystem: events and transitions over time in the child's life and in society (e.g. parents' divorce, shift to digital schooling, or the death of a grandparent).

example.q: Place each in Bronfenbrenner's systems: (a) Rohit's mother's office cuts salaries; (b) Rohit's teacher and parents meet monthly; (c) Indian cultural respect for elders; (d) Rohit's family moves cities when he is 10.
steps: (a) Affects Rohit through his mother; he isn't part of the office → exosystem.
(b) Link between two microsystems → mesosystem.
(c) Wider culture and values → macrosystem.
(d) A life transition over time → chronosystem.
example.answer: (a) exosystem, (b) mesosystem, (c) macrosystem, (d) chronosystem

learn.reallife: The Right to Education Act (a macrosystem/exosystem influence) changed which school millions of children attend, which then changed their peers and teachers (their microsystem).

topics.title: Sinha's ecological model, culture and developmental stages

learn.hook: An Indian child's world isn't just home and school; it is also a crowded joint family, the neighbourhood chai shop and the family's social and economic position. Durganand Sinha built a model for exactly this.
points: Durganand Sinha's ecological model of the development of the Indian child pictures the environment as two concentric layers.
The upper, most visible layer: home, school and peer group, which the child directly experiences.
The surrounding layer: the wider social and physical conditions such as the family's social and economic status, crowding and availability of facilities; the two layers interact and change over time.
Culture shapes developmental goals and parenting: for example, many Indian families value interdependence and respect for elders, while some other cultures stress early independence.
Developmental stages (prenatal, infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) each come with developmental tasks: skills and behaviour patterns a society expects at that stage.

example.q: Which layer of Sinha's model? (a) Riya's peer group at school; (b) her family living in a one-room house in a crowded area.
steps: (a) Peer group is directly experienced → upper (visible) layer.
(b) Crowding and living conditions are wider conditions → surrounding layer.
example.answer: (a) upper/visible layer, (b) surrounding layer

learn.reallife: In many Indian homes grandparents help raise children, which reflects a cultural macro-goal of interdependence; developmental psychologists in India study how this shapes children's social skills.

learn.hook: For about nine months before you were born, you were already developing at astonishing speed, and your mother's diet, health and stress were part of the story.
points: The prenatal period runs from conception to birth (about nine months). It has three periods: germinal (about the first two weeks), embryonic (about 2 to 8 weeks, when major organs form) and fetal (from about 2 months until birth).
Teratogens are environmental agents that can cause birth defects: maternal diseases (e.g. rubella/German measles, HIV/AIDS), drugs, alcohol, tobacco, radiation and pollution.
The mother's nutrition, emotional state (prolonged stress) and age (very young or older mothers face higher risks) also influence prenatal development.
Good prenatal care (nutrition, check-ups, avoiding harmful substances) supports healthy development.

example.q: A pregnant woman continues smoking and also has prolonged high stress. Identify the risk factors and their category.
steps: Tobacco is a harmful substance → teratogen.
Prolonged stress is a maternal emotional factor.
Both can affect prenatal development.
example.answer: Tobacco = teratogen; stress = maternal emotional state.

learn.reallife: Under the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana and Mission Indradhanush, pregnant women in India receive support for nutrition and immunisation, protecting babies during the prenatal period.

topics.title: Infancy: reflexes, motor and sensory development

learn.hook: Stroke a newborn's cheek and she turns her head and opens her mouth. Nobody taught her that. Newborns arrive pre-loaded with survival reflexes.
points: Reflexes are automatic, unlearned responses with survival value: rooting (turns head and opens mouth when cheek is touched), sucking (sucks object placed in mouth), Moro (startle: throws arms outward at a sudden loud noise or loss of support), Babinski (toes fan out when the sole is stroked), grasping (grips an object placed in the palm), blinking (closes eyes to bright light or puff of air).
Motor development follows milestones: rolling over, sitting, crawling, standing, walking.
Cephalocaudal trend: development proceeds from head to foot (head control comes before walking). Proximodistal trend: from the centre of the body outwards (arm control before finger control).
Newborns can see (vision is blurry at first), hear (they recognise the mother's voice), smell (recognise the mother's smell), taste (prefer sweet) and are sensitive to touch and pain.

example.q: A baby can hold her head up at 2 months, sit at about 6 months and walk at around a year. She can wave her whole arm long before she can pick up a raisin with thumb and finger. Name the two trends.
steps: Head control → sitting → walking: top to bottom → cephalocaudal.
Arm control before finger control: centre to periphery → proximodistal.
example.answer: Cephalocaudal and proximodistal trends

learn.reallife: Paediatricians at government hospitals check newborn reflexes like rooting and Moro soon after birth; their presence (and later disappearance) is a sign of healthy nervous-system development.

topics.title: Infancy: sensorimotor thought, attachment and temperament

learn.hook: Hide a toy under a dupatta in front of a 4-month-old and she stops looking for it, as if it has vanished. A year-old baby lifts the cloth. Something big has happened in her mind.
points: Piaget's sensorimotor stage (birth to about 2 years): infants understand the world through senses and actions (looking, grasping, sucking). A key achievement is object permanence, knowing that objects continue to exist when out of sight.

Attachment is the close emotional bond between the infant and the caregiver. Harlow's study: infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth 'mother' rather than a wire 'mother' that gave milk, which shows the importance of contact comfort, not just feeding.
Securely attached infants use the caregiver as a safe base to explore; insecurely attached infants may avoid the caregiver or show anxious, clingy behaviour.
Erikson's first stage, trust vs mistrust: warm, consistent care builds a sense of trust; neglect or inconsistency leads to mistrust.

Temperament is the baby's typical style of responding: easy (regular routines, cheerful), difficult (irregular, intense negative reactions) and slow-to-warm-up (low activity, adjusts slowly to new situations).

example.q: Harlow's monkeys spent most time on the cloth mother and went to the wire mother only to feed. When frightened, they ran to the cloth mother. What does this show?
steps: Feeding alone did not create the bond.
Comfort from soft contact was preferred, especially when afraid.
So attachment depends on contact comfort, not just food.
example.answer: Attachment is based on contact comfort, not just feeding.

learn.reallife: Kangaroo mother care, promoted in Indian hospitals for low-birth-weight babies, uses skin-to-skin contact, which supports warmth, feeding and attachment.

topics.title: Childhood: physical growth and Piaget's preoperational and concrete stages

learn.hook: Pour juice from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin one in front of a 4-year-old and she'll say there's 'more juice now'. An 8-year-old will roll her eyes: 'It's the same, you just poured it!'
points: Physical development in childhood is slower than in infancy; gross motor skills (running, jumping) and fine motor skills (writing, buttoning) improve, and handedness becomes established.

Preoperational stage (about 2 to 7 years): symbolic thought appears (using one thing to stand for another, e.g. pretend play with a stick as a horse); thought is egocentric (cannot take another's viewpoint) and shows animism (believing lifeless objects are alive).

Limits of preoperational thought: centration (focusing on one feature, e.g. height of liquid), irreversibility (cannot mentally reverse an action) and lack of conservation; intuitive thought (about 4-7 years) brings many 'why?' questions.

Concrete operational stage (about 7 to 11 years): children understand conservation and reversibility, can classify and seriate (arrange in order by size), and reason logically about concrete objects, but not yet about abstract ideas.
Exam tip: identify the stage from the behaviour described (pretend play/egocentrism → preoperational; conservation/seriation → concrete operational).

example.q: Five-year-old Tara says the moon follows her car, and thinks her teddy feels sad when left alone. Which stage, and which features?
steps: Believing the moon follows her = egocentrism (world centred on her).
Teddy feels sad = animism (lifeless object has feelings).
Both are typical of the preoperational stage.
example.answer: Preoperational stage: egocentrism and animism

learn.reallife: When a Class 3 child arranges her pencils from shortest to longest and sorts Diwali sweets by type, she is showing seriation and classification: concrete operational skills.

topics.title: Childhood: self, Erikson's early stages, moral development and influences

learn.hook: A 3-year-old insists, 'I'll pour the water myself!' A 9-year-old proudly shows her science project. Both are working through life stages that Erik Erikson mapped out.
points: In childhood, children form a self-concept (how they describe themselves), learn gender roles (behaviour society expects of boys and girls) and develop self-esteem (how they value themselves).

Erikson's childhood stages: autonomy vs shame and doubt (toddlerhood: doing things oneself), initiative vs guilt (preschool years: planning and trying activities), industry vs inferiority (school years: mastering skills, feeling competent).

Kohlberg's levels of moral reasoning: preconventional (right and wrong judged by rewards and punishments), conventional (following rules, laws and others' approval), postconventional (based on universal ethical principles and personal conscience).
Parents (warm, supportive parenting helps self-esteem) and peers (who teach cooperation, competition and social rules) strongly influence children's development.

example.q: Asked why one shouldn't steal, (a) Raju, 6, says 'You'll get beaten'; (b) Simran, 13, says 'It's against the law and people will think badly of you'; (c) an adult says 'Taking what isn't yours violates others' rights.' Identify Kohlberg's levels.
steps: (a) Focus on punishment → preconventional.
(b) Focus on rules and approval → conventional.
(c) Focus on universal principles → postconventional.
example.answer: (a) preconventional, (b) conventional, (c) postconventional

learn.reallife: School activities like Bal Sabhas, science fairs and sports days give children chances to feel competent, which builds industry rather than inferiority.

topics.title: Adolescence: puberty, formal operations and egocentrism

learn.hook: One pimple and you're sure the whole class is staring. Feel invincible on a bike without a helmet? Psychologists have names for both feelings, and they are very normal in adolescence.
points: Adolescence is the transition from childhood to adulthood, beginning around puberty and extending into the late teens (roughly 12 to 18-20 years in many accounts).

Puberty brings a growth spurt, the development of secondary sex characteristics (e.g. breasts in girls, facial hair and voice change in boys), and in girls menarche (the first menstruation). Early or late maturation can affect self-image and adjustment differently for boys and girls.

Piaget's formal operational stage (about 11 years onwards): abstract thinking, hypothetical-deductive reasoning (forming and testing hypotheses systematically) and idealism (imagining ideal worlds and comparing reality with them).
Adolescent egocentrism: imaginary audience (believing others are constantly watching and judging you) and personal fable (believing you are unique and invulnerable, 'it won't happen to me').
Adolescents begin to question values and rules; moral reasoning can become more principled.

example.q: Classify: (a) Neha is sure everyone noticed her new haircut and is talking about it; (b) Ravi rides fast without a helmet thinking 'accidents happen to others'; (c) Sana argues about how a perfectly fair society would work.
steps: (a) Belief that others are watching = imaginary audience.
(b) Feeling invulnerable = personal fable.
(c) Thinking about ideal possibilities = idealism (formal operational thought).
example.answer: (a) imaginary audience, (b) personal fable, (c) idealism/formal operational thought

learn.reallife: Debates in school parliaments and Model UN, where teens argue about policies for ideal societies, put formal operational, hypothetical reasoning to work.

teach.praise: Chirp! Puberty, abstract formal operational thought, imaginary audience and personal fable. Teens are fascinating!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the two forms of adolescent egocentrism?

learn.hook: 'Science or Arts? Engineer, artist or entrepreneur? Who am I, really?' If these questions keep you up at night, Erikson would say you're doing exactly what adolescents are supposed to do.
points: Erikson's adolescent stage is identity vs role confusion: forming a stable sense of who one is (values, goals, career). Failure leads to confusion about one's roles.
Identity is shaped by family, peers, culture, school and vocational choices; supportive families and opportunities to explore help.

Major concerns: delinquency (law-breaking acts by adolescents), substance abuse (harmful use of alcohol, tobacco or drugs) and eating disorders: anorexia nervosa (severe food restriction with intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image) and bulimia nervosa (episodes of binge eating followed by attempts to prevent weight gain).
These problems are not a sign of weak character; they have psychological, social and biological roots and can be treated. Early help from parents, teachers, counsellors or doctors matters.
Coping and support: healthy routines, talking to trusted people, peer support, counselling and helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416) help adolescents manage stress.

example.q: Priya, 16, feels confused about her career; her parents want medicine, she loves design. How can she work towards a clear identity?
steps: Identity vs role confusion: she needs to explore options.
Talk openly with parents; try internships or workshops in design and science.
Speak with a school counsellor about interests and aptitude.
Make a choice based on her values and abilities.
example.answer: By exploring options, talking with parents and a counsellor, and choosing based on her values: building identity rather than role confusion.

learn.reallife: Many CBSE schools now have counsellors and wellness teachers, and Tele-MANAS (14416) provides free 24×7 mental-health support in many Indian languages, including for teenagers.

learn.hook: Your parents juggle office deadlines, EMIs and your school fees; your grandparents swap stories of the past. Development keeps posing new challenges long after school ends.
points: Early adulthood: tasks include choosing and settling in a career, marriage, and parenthood. Erikson: intimacy vs isolation, forming close, committed relationships.

Middle adulthood: physical changes (e.g. declining vision); in women, menopause (end of menstruation). Erikson: generativity vs stagnation, contributing to the next generation through work, parenting or mentoring. The 'empty nest' can occur when grown children leave home.

Old age: retirement, physical slowing, some decline in speed of cognitive processing (while knowledge and wisdom may remain), and often widowhood. Erikson: integrity vs despair, looking back on life with satisfaction or regret.
Attitudes to ageing are changing; family support protects against loneliness, while the shift to nuclear families can increase isolation of the elderly.
Activity idea: interview a grandparent about how their life changed from childhood to old age and note the developmental tasks at each stage.

example.q: Mr. Sharma, 68, retired two years ago. He mentors young teachers and feels proud of his life, though he misses his late wife. Which Erikson stage is he in and how is he handling it?
steps: At 68 he is in old age.
Erikson's crisis then is integrity vs despair.
Feeling proud of life and staying engaged shows integrity, though grief is natural.
example.answer: Integrity vs despair; he shows integrity.

learn.reallife: The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 and community day-care centres for elders reflect India's response to loneliness and support needs in old age.

topics.title: Knowing the world: stimuli, sensation and perception

learn.hook: In a crowded Chandni Chowk lane, a thousand sights, smells and sounds hit you at once, yet you instantly recognise the smell of jalebis and your friend's voice calling you. Three processes make that possible.
points: We know the world through three processes working together: sensation (receiving stimuli through sense organs), attention (selecting some stimuli) and perception (interpreting them).
Sensation is the detection of a stimulus by sense organs and its conversion into nerve signals; perception is the process of organising and giving meaning to those signals.
Stimuli vary in type (light, sound, smell, taste, touch) and in features such as intensity, duration and frequency.

Each sense organ has receptors specialised for a particular kind of stimulus: the eye for light, the ear for sound waves, the nose for chemicals in air, the tongue for chemicals in food, the skin for pressure, temperature and pain.

example.q: While crossing a road you hear a horn, turn, and recognise it as an approaching auto-rickshaw. Separate sensation, attention and perception.
steps: Sound waves reach the ears and are detected → sensation.
You turn towards the horn, ignoring other noises → attention.
You interpret the sound as 'an auto is coming' → perception.
example.answer: Hearing the horn = sensation; turning to it = attention; recognising it as an auto = perception.

learn.reallife: Railway level-crossing signals combine bright flashing lights and loud bells, stimuli of high intensity on two different sense organs, so they are sensed, attended to and correctly perceived as danger.

topics.title: Sense modalities: external and internal senses

learn.hook: Close your eyes and touch your nose with your finger. How did your finger know where to go? You used senses most people never list.
points: Humans have seven sense modalities: five external senses (vision - eyes, hearing - ears, smell - nose, taste - tongue, touch/skin senses - skin) and two internal senses.
Kinesthetic sense: gives information about the position and movement of body parts relative to each other; its receptors are in the muscles, joints and ligaments.
Vestibular sense: gives information about balance and the body's position in relation to gravity; its receptors are in the inner ear (semicircular canals and vestibular sacs).
Internal senses work without our awareness most of the time, which is why we rarely notice them unless something goes wrong (e.g. dizziness).

example.q: Which sense is mainly involved? (a) A gymnast keeps her balance on a beam. (b) You know your arm is raised without looking. (c) You feel the warmth of a cup of chai.
steps: (a) Balance relative to gravity → vestibular.
(b) Position of a body part → kinesthetic.
(c) Temperature on the skin → touch/skin senses.
example.answer: (a) vestibular, (b) kinesthetic, (c) skin (touch)

learn.reallife: Astronauts like those trained for ISRO's Gaganyaan feel disoriented in microgravity because their vestibular sense, built for Earth's gravity, sends confusing signals.
