learn.hook: A mosquito buzzing in a silent room is unbearable; the same buzz at a wedding is unnoticed. Our senses have limits, and those limits can be measured.
points: Our sense organs have functional limitations: they respond only to stimuli within a certain range (e.g. we cannot hear very high-pitched dog whistles).
Absolute threshold (absolute limen): the minimum value (intensity) of a stimulus needed for it to be noticed. It is not fixed; it varies across people and from time to time for the same person.

Difference threshold (difference limen): the minimum difference between two stimuli needed for them to be noticed as different; this smallest noticeable difference is called the just noticeable difference (JND).
Psychophysics is the study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce.

example.q: Meena can just hear a whisper at 3 metres but not at 4 metres. Later she finds that she can tell a 1 kg bag from a heavier one only when the difference is at least 50 g (1.05 kg); a 1.02 kg bag feels the same as 1 kg. Name the two thresholds involved.
steps: The faintest whisper she can detect = minimum intensity for detection → absolute threshold.
The smallest weight difference she can tell apart → difference threshold (JND).
example.answer: Whisper = absolute threshold; weight difference = difference threshold/JND.

learn.reallife: Sweet-shop owners know that customers rarely notice a very small change in the size of a laddoo, because the change is below the JND, which is why such changes go unnoticed.

topics.title: Attention: nature, focus and fringe, types and span

learn.hook: While you read this, you aren't aware of your shirt touching your skin, until now. Attention is the spotlight that decides what reaches your awareness.
points: Attention is the process of selecting certain stimuli from among the many that reach us. It rests on arousal (a general level of activation) and involves alertness (readiness to deal with stimuli), concentration (focusing on some objects while excluding others) and search (actively looking for something).
The field of attention has a focus (centre: the object most clearly in awareness) and a fringe (margin: objects only vaguely noticed).

Types of attention: selective (choosing one stimulus among many), sustained (keeping attention on something for a long time) and divided (attending to two or more tasks at once, which becomes easier when tasks are practised and automatic).
Span of attention: the number of objects one can attend to in a brief glimpse.

example.q: Raghav is listening to a lecture while taking notes, glancing occasionally at a friend's text message. Identify focus, fringe and the type of attention.
steps: Lecture content is most clearly in awareness → focus.
The text message is vaguely noticed → fringe.
Listening and writing together → divided attention (note-taking has become fairly automatic).
example.answer: Focus: lecture; fringe: phone message; divided attention.

topics.title: Selective attention: external and internal factors

learn.hook: Why do ads on TV play louder than the show, use bright colours and moving logos, and why do you suddenly notice every food stall when you're hungry? The secrets lie in factors that grab attention.
points: External factors (features of the stimulus): size (bigger), intensity (louder/brighter), motion (moving objects), novelty (new or unusual), colour, and moderate complexity attract attention; human faces and voices also capture attention easily.
Internal factors are of two kinds: motivational (needs and drives, e.g. a hungry person notices the smell of food) and cognitive (interest, attitude and preparatory set).
Preparatory set: a mental readiness to respond to a particular stimulus, e.g. a sprinter waiting for the starter's gun.
Exam tip: when asked for factors of selective attention, separate them into external (stimulus) and internal (person: motivational and cognitive).

example.q: Classify: (a) A flashing red light on a billboard; (b) a cricket fan notices a TV score even in a crowd; (c) a thirsty traveller spots a water cooler.
steps: (a) Feature of the stimulus (intensity, colour, motion) → external.
(b) Interest of the person → internal, cognitive.
(c) Need of the person → internal, motivational.
example.answer: (a) external, (b) internal-cognitive, (c) internal-motivational

learn.reallife: Indian Railways uses large, brightly coloured, flashing displays and loud announcements at stations so that passengers' attention is captured despite the crowd and noise.

learn.hook: At a noisy party you are deep in conversation, yet the moment someone across the room says your name, you hear it. If you were blocking out other conversations, how did your name get through?
points: Filter theory (Broadbent): many stimuli enter a selective filter, which lets only one through to short-term memory for further processing; the rest are blocked.
Filter-attenuation theory (Treisman): unattended messages are not blocked completely but weakened (attenuated); strong or meaningful messages, such as your own name, can still get through.

Multimode theory (Johnston and Heinz): attention is flexible, and selection can occur at different stages of processing, early (sensory) or late (meaning); the later the selection, the more mental capacity it requires.
Exam tip: Broadbent = block; Treisman = weaken; Johnston and Heinz = flexible stage.

example.q: Which theory best explains the 'cocktail party effect', where you notice your name in an unattended conversation?
steps: Broadbent says unattended messages are blocked, so your name shouldn't get through.
Treisman says unattended messages are only weakened, so a highly meaningful one (your name) can pass.
So Treisman's theory explains it better.
example.answer: Treisman's filter-attenuation theory

learn.reallife: Call-centre staff in Gurugram learn to tune into one caller while weakened background chatter keeps reaching them; an urgent word like 'fire' still breaks through, as Treisman predicted.

learn.hook: Picture a radar operator watching a screen through the night for the rare blip of an unknown aircraft. Most of the time nothing happens, and that is exactly what makes the job so hard.
points: Sustained attention (vigilance) is the ability to concentrate on a task for a long period, e.g. radar operators, security guards, or lifeguards.

Factors influencing sustained attention: sensory modality (performance is better for auditory than for visual stimuli), clarity of stimuli (intense, long-lasting stimuli are easier to keep track of), temporal uncertainty (stimuli at regular, expected intervals are attended better) and spatial uncertainty (stimuli at a fixed place are easier to monitor).

Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a condition beginning in childhood whose main features are inattention, hyperactivity (excessive restlessness and movement) and impulsivity (acting without thinking).
ADHD is not caused by laziness or bad character; with proper assessment, behavioural support, parent and teacher guidance, and sometimes medication, children manage it well.

example.q: A security guard misses an intruder at 3 a.m. Suggest two changes to the task based on the factors of sustained attention.
steps: Use an auditory alarm along with the camera feed (auditory signals sustain attention better).
Make the camera alerts clearer and fixed in one corner of the screen (reduces spatial uncertainty).
Give regular short breaks to reduce fatigue.
example.answer: Add sound alerts, make signals clearer and at fixed locations, and schedule breaks.

learn.reallife: Lifeguards on Mumbai's Juhu beach work in rotations because sustained visual attention over a wide, changing area (high spatial uncertainty) drops quickly over time.

learn.hook: 'Yuo cna raed tihs sntenece eevn thuogh the lttres are jmbuled.' Your brain doesn't just add up letters; it guesses using what it already knows.
points: Perception is the process of giving meaning to sensory input, recognising objects and events; it is an active, constructive process.
Bottom-up processing: recognition begins with details (parts) and builds up to the whole, e.g. identifying a new symbol by its lines and curves.
Top-down processing: recognition starts from the whole, using expectations, knowledge and context to identify parts, e.g. reading messy handwriting from context.
The perceiver's motivation and needs affect perception: hungry people tend to see ambiguous figures as food-related; needs make some interpretations more likely.

example.q: You see 'I3' between 'A' and 'C' and read it as 'B'; between '12' and '14' you read it as '13'. Which processing explains this?
steps: The marks are identical in both cases.
Context (letters vs numbers) guides the interpretation.
Using expectations and context = top-down processing.
example.answer: Top-down processing

learn.reallife: Radiologists at AIIMS combine bottom-up scanning of every shadow on a scan with top-down knowledge of what tumours usually look like, which is why experience matters.

topics.title: The perceiver: set, cognitive style and culture

learn.hook: Show the same 'Rorschach-like' ink blot to an engineer, a farmer and an artist. You'll get a bridge, a cloud before rain and a dancer. What we perceive depends on who we are.
points: Expectations or perceptual set: a readiness to perceive in a particular way, based on past experience and context. E.g. if you have just read a list of animals, an ambiguous figure is more likely to be seen as an animal.

Cognitive styles: consistent ways of organising and processing information. Field-dependent people perceive objects as part of the whole surrounding field; field-independent people can separate an object from its surroundings (e.g. finding a hidden figure in a complex design).
Socio-cultural background and experiences influence what we notice and how we interpret it, e.g. which colours or shapes are familiar, or how pictures are read.
The perceiver is therefore not a passive receiver: needs, expectations, cognitive style and culture all shape perception.

example.q: Ravi quickly finds a small triangle hidden inside a complex pattern, while Arun sees only the overall pattern. Describe their cognitive styles.
steps: Ravi separates the figure from its surrounding field → field-independent.
Arun perceives the pattern as a whole and can't pull out the part → field-dependent.
example.answer: Ravi: field-independent; Arun: field-dependent

learn.hook: Look at a vase and suddenly it's two faces in profile; look again and it's a vase. The picture hasn't changed, but your brain's organisation of it has.
points: Gestalt psychologists (Wertheimer, Kohler, Koffka) held that we perceive organised wholes or forms (gestalts); the whole is more than, and different from, the sum of its parts.
Figure-ground segregation: we see an object (figure) standing out against a background (ground). In reversible figures (e.g. Rubin's vase-faces) figure and ground can switch.

Principles of organisation: proximity (things near each other are grouped), similarity (similar things are grouped), continuity (we follow smooth, continuous lines), closure (we fill gaps to see complete figures).

Further principles: smallness (smaller areas tend to be seen as figures against a larger background), symmetry (symmetrical areas tend to be seen as figures), surroundedness (areas enclosed by others tend to be seen as figures).
These principles help design logos, signs and road markings that are seen quickly and correctly.

example.q: Name the principle: (a) A circle with small gaps is still seen as a circle. (b) In a grid of dots, rows of red and blue dots are seen as red and blue rows. (c) Dots placed in pairs are seen as pairs.
steps: (a) Filling in missing parts → closure.
(b) Grouping by colour → similarity.
(c) Grouping by nearness → proximity.
example.answer: (a) closure, (b) similarity, (c) proximity

learn.reallife: The Tricolour's Ashoka Chakra, many company logos and even rangoli patterns rely on symmetry, closure and figure-ground so that they are recognised instantly.

topics.title: Perceiving depth and distance: monocular and binocular cues

learn.hook: The image on your retina is flat, like a photograph, yet you can judge exactly when to catch a cricket ball flying towards you. Your brain reads depth from many clues.
points: The retina receives 2-D images, but we perceive a 3-D world using depth cues.

Monocular (psychological) cues, usable with one eye and used by artists: relative size (smaller image = farther), interposition or overlap (an object blocking another is nearer), linear perspective (parallel lines seem to converge in the distance).

More monocular cues: aerial perspective (distant objects look hazy and bluish), light and shade (shadows show depth and shape), relative height (objects higher in the visual field appear farther), texture gradient (texture becomes finer and denser with distance), motion parallax (when we move, near objects seem to move fast in the opposite direction and far ones slowly in the same direction).

Binocular (physiological) cues, as grouped in NCERT: retinal or binocular disparity (each eye gets a slightly different image; greater disparity means nearer), convergence (eyes turn inward for near objects) and accommodation (the lens changes thickness to focus; more for near objects).
Exam tip: if a cue works in a painting or photograph, it is monocular.

example.q: In a photo of railway tracks, the rails seem to meet at the horizon, the far hills look hazy, and a train partly hides a signal post. Name the three cues.
steps: Rails converging → linear perspective.
Hazy distant hills → aerial perspective.
Train blocking the post → interposition (overlap).
All are monocular cues.
example.answer: Linear perspective, aerial perspective and interposition (monocular cues)

learn.hook: Your friend walking away from you down the corridor shrinks on your retina to half size, then a quarter. Yet you never think she is turning into a tiny person.
points: Perceptual constancy: we perceive objects as relatively stable in size, shape and brightness even though the retinal image changes with distance, angle and lighting.
Size constancy: an object is perceived as the same size whether it is near or far, though its retinal image shrinks with distance.
Shape constancy: an object is perceived as the same shape even when seen from different angles (a door is seen as rectangular even when its image is a trapezium as it opens).

Brightness constancy: an object's brightness is perceived as relatively constant under different illumination (white paper looks white in sunlight and in dim light, because it reflects the same proportion of light).

example.q: Identify the constancy: (a) A cricket ball looks the same size when thrown from the boundary. (b) A plate looks round from the side though its image is oval. (c) Coal looks black even in bright sunlight.
steps: (a) Size stays stable despite distance → size constancy.
(b) Shape stays stable despite angle → shape constancy.
(c) Darkness stays stable despite lighting → brightness constancy.
example.answer: (a) size, (b) shape, (c) brightness constancy

learn.reallife: Pilots landing at Leh or Kolkata must judge runway shape and size from changing angles; perceptual constancies keep the runway looking like the same rectangle throughout.

topics.title: Illusions: Muller-Lyer and the phi phenomenon

learn.hook: Two lines of exactly equal length; one with arrowheads pointing in, one with tails pointing out. Measure them with a ruler and you still can't stop seeing one as longer.
points: Illusions are misperceptions of real stimuli: the stimulus is present but is perceived incorrectly. Many illusions are experienced by most people (universal) and persist even when we know they are false.
Muller-Lyer illusion (a geometrical illusion): two lines of equal length look unequal; the one with outward-pointing fins (like tails) looks longer than the one with inward-pointing arrowheads.

Phi phenomenon (apparent movement illusion): when stationary lights are switched on and off in quick succession, we perceive movement. Films and animation work this way: still frames shown rapidly appear as continuous motion.
Illusions differ from hallucinations, which are perceptions without any real external stimulus.

example.q: Festival lights on a building seem to 'run' along the edge, though each bulb only switches on and off in place. Name the illusion and explain.
steps: No bulb actually moves.
Bulbs flash in quick succession.
We perceive movement where there is none → apparent movement.
example.answer: Phi phenomenon (apparent movement illusion)

learn.reallife: Every Bollywood film you watch in a theatre is a sequence of still frames, typically 24 per second, which your brain stitches into smooth motion through apparent movement.

learn.hook: If you grew up surrounded by rectangular rooms, straight roads and sharp corners, you may be more fooled by the Muller-Lyer lines than someone who grew up in round huts among open fields.
points: Perception is shaped by cultural experience: people from different cultures can differ in how strongly they experience certain illusions.
Segall, Campbell and Herskovits found that susceptibility to the Muller-Lyer illusion varied across cultural groups.

Carpentered-world idea: people living in environments full of rectangles, straight lines and right-angled corners (buildings, furniture) are more susceptible to the Muller-Lyer illusion than people from less 'carpentered' environments, because they learn to read angles as depth cues.
Research, including studies with rural and tribal groups in India, shows that schooling, exposure to pictures and ecological background affect how people read depth cues in 2-D pictures.

example.q: Group A lives in a city of rectangular buildings; Group B lives in a rural area with round huts and few straight lines. Which group is likely to be more susceptible to the Muller-Lyer illusion and why?
steps: City life gives constant experience of corners and straight edges.
This trains people to read angle fins as depth cues.
So Group A is likely to be more susceptible (carpentered-world idea).
example.answer: Group A, because of experience with a carpentered world

learn.reallife: Health-education posters used in different regions of India are tested with local audiences first, because people unfamiliar with certain drawing styles may not read depth or perspective in pictures as designers intend.

learn.hook: Riding a bicycle, fearing the dentist's chair, typing on a phone keyboard without looking: none of these came pre-installed. You learnt them. But is every change in behaviour learning?
points: Learning is a key process through which behaviour changes as a result of experience; much of what we do is learnt.
Definition: learning is any relatively permanent change in behaviour or behavioural potential produced by experience or practice.
Changes due to maturation (e.g. a baby starting to walk), fatigue, drugs, illness or injury are NOT learning, because they don't come from experience/practice or are not relatively permanent.
Features: learning always involves experience; the changes are relatively permanent; learning cannot be seen directly, so it is inferred from performance.
Learning is a process with a sequence of psychological events, e.g. measuring performance before (pre-test), practising, and measuring after (post-test) to see the change.

example.q: Which of these is learning? (a) Sleepy after a heavy lunch you type slowly. (b) After months of practice you type 60 words per minute. (c) A child's voice deepens at puberty.
steps: (a) Temporary change due to fatigue → not learning.
(b) Relatively permanent change from practice → learning.
(c) Change due to maturation → not learning.
example.answer: Only (b) is learning.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways loco pilots train for months in simulators before driving real trains; their improved, lasting performance after practice is learning, while a bad day due to tiredness is not.

topics.title: Paradigms of learning and Pavlov's experiment

learn.hook: In the 1900s, Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs when he noticed something odd: the dogs started drooling before the food arrived, at the sound of footsteps. That accident opened up a whole field.
points: Types (paradigms) of learning: classical conditioning, operant (instrumental) conditioning, observational learning, cognitive learning, verbal learning and skill learning.
The simplest kind of learning is conditioning, which is associative learning: learning that two events go together.
Pavlov's experiment: a dog was harnessed and its saliva measured through a tube. A bell was sounded and food was given just after. After several pairings, the bell alone made the dog salivate.
So the dog learnt an association between the bell and food: this is classical conditioning.

example.q: Describe Pavlov's procedure in three phases.
steps: Before conditioning: food → salivation; bell → no salivation.
During conditioning: bell is sounded and then food is given, repeatedly.
After conditioning: bell alone → salivation.
example.answer: Bell paired repeatedly with food until the bell alone produced salivation.

learn.reallife: Hear the ting of a Swiggy or Zomato notification and your stomach rumbles? The sound has been paired with food so often that it alone triggers hunger signals, a modern Pavlovian effect.

topics.title: US, UR, CS and CR: acquisition of conditioned responses

learn.hook: A child gets an injection and cries. Next visit, she cries the moment she sees the white coat. Psychologists can label every part of that sad little chain.
points: Unconditioned stimulus (US): naturally produces a response without learning (food). Unconditioned response (UR): the natural, unlearned response to the US (salivation to food).

Conditioned stimulus (CS): an originally neutral stimulus that, after pairing with the US, produces a response (bell). Conditioned response (CR): the learned response to the CS (salivation to the bell).
Acquisition: the CR is acquired through repeated pairings of the CS with the US; the CS must reliably predict the US.
Everyday examples: fear of a dentist's drill sound, liking a song linked to happy times, feeling hungry at the sight of a restaurant logo.

example.q: A child is stung by a bee (pain, crying). Later, the buzzing sound alone makes her afraid. Label US, UR, CS and CR.
steps: Bee sting naturally causes pain/fear → US.
Fear/crying to the sting → UR.
Buzzing sound, originally neutral, paired with the sting → CS.
Fear to the buzzing alone → CR.
example.answer: US = sting; UR = fear to sting; CS = buzzing; CR = fear to buzzing

learn.reallife: Many people feel anxious at the sound of an exam-hall bell years after school: the bell (CS) was repeatedly paired with high-stakes tests (US).

teach.praise: Chirp! US food, UR salivation, CS bell, CR salivation to the bell. I can label any conditioning now!

learn.hook: Ring the bell after the food, and Pavlov's dogs barely learn anything. Ring it just before, and they learn fast. Timing is everything in classical conditioning.
points: Time relations between CS and US: simultaneous (CS and US begin together), delayed (CS begins first and stays on until the US begins), trace (CS begins and ends before the US begins, leaving a memory trace), backward (US is presented before the CS).
Delayed conditioning is the most effective; backward conditioning is the least effective (learning is rare).

Type of US: appetitive US (pleasant, e.g. food, water) produces approach responses; aversive US (painful or harmful, e.g. shock, loud noise) produces avoidance or escape responses. Aversive conditioning is often established very quickly, sometimes in one trial.
Intensity of the CS: a more intense CS leads to faster acquisition, i.e. fewer trials are needed.

example.q: A light (CS) comes on and stays on; after 2 seconds food (US) arrives, and the light goes off. In another set-up, the light flashes for 1 second and goes off, then food comes 5 seconds later. Name both procedures.
steps: Set-up 1: CS starts first and overlaps until the US begins → delayed conditioning.
Set-up 2: CS ends before the US starts, a gap is left → trace conditioning.
example.answer: Set-up 1: delayed; set-up 2: trace

learn.reallife: Ad makers place the brand jingle just before the happy moment in an ad, not after, using the delayed-conditioning logic that the CS must predict the US.

topics.title: Operant conditioning: Skinner and the Skinner box

learn.hook: A hungry rat in a box presses a lever by accident; a food pellet drops. It presses again. Soon it's pressing like a pro. B.F. Skinner turned this simple scene into one of psychology's biggest ideas.
points: Operant conditioning was first investigated by B.F. Skinner. Operants are voluntary behaviours that 'operate' on the environment; they are controlled by their consequences.
Skinner box: a hungry rat placed in a box with a lever. When it presses the lever, a food pellet is delivered. Over trials, lever pressing increases.
It is also called instrumental conditioning because the response is instrumental (the means) in getting the reward.
Reinforcement is any stimulus or event that increases the probability of the response it follows; it strengthens the response.

example.q: Explain the Skinner box experiment in terms of response, consequence and learning.
steps: Response: the rat presses the lever (a voluntary operant).
Consequence: food pellet (reinforcer) follows.
Learning: the probability of lever pressing increases with repeated reinforcement.
example.answer: The lever press (operant) is strengthened because it is followed by food (reinforcement).

learn.reallife: Loyalty programmes from airlines or supermarkets reward you with points every time you buy; your buying behaviour (operant) gets reinforced by consequences.

topics.title: Reinforcers: positive, negative, primary and secondary

learn.hook: You take a painkiller, the headache vanishes, and next time you reach for the same tablet faster. Nothing pleasant was given; something unpleasant was removed. That still counts as reinforcement.
points: Positive reinforcers: pleasant consequences (food, money, praise) whose presentation strengthens a response. Negative reinforcers: unpleasant or painful stimuli (noise, pain, cold); a response that removes, escapes or avoids them is strengthened (negative reinforcement).
Primary reinforcers are biological and unlearned (food, water, relief from pain); secondary reinforcers acquire value through association with primary ones (money, grades, praise, medals).
Number, amount and quality of reinforcement matter: more reinforced trials, a larger amount and a higher-quality reward generally lead to faster learning (up to a point).
Delay of reinforcement: the longer the delay between response and reinforcer, the slower and weaker the learning; immediate reinforcement works best.

example.q: Classify: (a) A child gets chocolate for finishing homework. (b) Fastening the seatbelt stops the car's annoying beep, so you buckle up sooner each time. (c) Money for good marks.
steps: (a) Pleasant consequence added → positive reinforcement; chocolate is a primary reinforcer.
(b) Unpleasant beep removed → negative reinforcement.
(c) Money's value is learned → secondary reinforcer (positive).
example.answer: (a) positive, primary; (b) negative reinforcement; (c) secondary (positive) reinforcer

learn.reallife: Cash rewards and instant UPI cashbacks work as secondary reinforcers; since they arrive immediately after payment, they strengthen the habit of digital payments faster than a delayed reward would.

learn.hook: Why do people keep scratching lottery tickets, refreshing social media, or calling a busy friend again and again? The secret is not how much they are rewarded, but on what schedule.
points: Continuous reinforcement: every correct response is reinforced. Partial (intermittent) reinforcement: only some responses are reinforced.

Fixed ratio (FR): reinforcement after a fixed number of responses (e.g. paid per 10 shirts stitched). Variable ratio (VR): after a varying, unpredictable number of responses (e.g. lottery, slot machines).

Fixed interval (FI): reinforcement for the first response after a fixed time period (e.g. monthly salary, a weekly test). Variable interval (VI): for the first response after varying time periods (e.g. surprise quizzes, checking for a message).

Partial reinforcement produces greater resistance to extinction than continuous reinforcement: responses learned with partial reinforcement last longer when rewards stop. Variable schedules produce the most persistent responding.
Continuous reinforcement is best for fast initial learning; partial reinforcement is best for maintaining a behaviour.

example.q: Identify the schedule: (a) A farm worker paid ₹100 for every 20 kg of tea leaves plucked. (b) A teacher gives surprise tests on unpredictable days. (c) A salesperson gets a bonus after an unpredictable number of sales.
steps: (a) Reward after a fixed number of responses → fixed ratio.
(b) Reward available after unpredictable time periods → variable interval.
(c) Reward after an unpredictable number of responses → variable ratio.
example.answer: (a) FR, (b) VI, (c) VR

learn.reallife: Cricket fans keep watching every ball because sixes and wickets come after unpredictable numbers of deliveries, a variable-ratio schedule that makes the behaviour hard to stop.

topics.title: Punishment, negative reinforcement, escape and avoidance

learn.hook: Board exam favourite: 'Negative reinforcement is a kind of punishment.' True or false? False, and examiners love that trap. Let's make sure you never fall into it.
points: Punishment: an aversive stimulus following a response, which decreases (weakens or suppresses) that response, e.g. a fine for littering.

Negative reinforcement: removal of an aversive stimulus following a response, which increases (strengthens) that response, e.g. taking a painkiller that removes a headache. So negative reinforcement is NOT punishment.
Escape conditioning: learning a response that ends an aversive situation that is already present (e.g. leaving a smoky room, opening an umbrella in the rain).
Avoidance conditioning: learning a response that prevents an aversive situation before it begins (e.g. leaving home early to avoid a traffic jam, carrying an umbrella when clouds gather).

example.q: Classify: (a) A student who talks in class has to stay back after school, and talks less. (b) Wearing earplugs stops the irritating construction noise, and you wear them more often. (c) Leaving for the station early to avoid missing the train.
steps: (a) Aversive consequence decreases the behaviour → punishment.
(b) Aversive noise removed, behaviour increases → negative reinforcement (escape).
(c) Response prevents the aversive event → avoidance conditioning.
example.answer: (a) punishment, (b) negative reinforcement (escape), (c) avoidance

learn.reallife: Traffic e-challans in Indian cities are punishment meant to decrease rash driving; a driver who slows down near cameras to avoid a challan is showing avoidance learning.

topics.title: Key learning processes: extinction, recovery, generalisation, discrimination, shaping

learn.hook: A puppy bitten by a large black dog starts fearing all black dogs, then all dogs. A circus elephant learns a complex trick one tiny step at a time. Same learning principles, different directions.
points: Extinction: the weakening and eventual disappearance of a learned response when reinforcement (or the US) is no longer given, e.g. the bell repeatedly sounded without food.
Spontaneous recovery: after extinction and a rest period, the extinguished response reappears when the CS is presented again (usually weaker).

Generalisation: responding in the same way to stimuli similar to the original CS (fear of one dog → fear of similar dogs). Discrimination: responding differently to different stimuli, e.g. responding only to the reinforced tone, not similar tones.
Shaping: reinforcing successive approximations, small steps closer and closer to the desired behaviour, until the complex behaviour is learned.
Chaining: linking a series of simple responses into a complex sequence, each step leading to the next (e.g. a dance routine).

example.q: Teaching a child to write her name: first she is praised for holding the pencil, then for drawing lines, then for forming each letter, finally for writing the whole name. What process is used?
steps: The final behaviour (writing the name) is complex.
Each small step closer to the goal is reinforced.
Reinforcing successive approximations = shaping.
example.answer: Shaping

learn.reallife: Dog-handling teams of the Indian Army train sniffer dogs to discriminate the smell of explosives from similar smells, after first teaching basic responses through shaping.

topics.title: Observational learning: Bandura's Bobo doll study

learn.hook: Nobody gives a toddler a reward for holding a phone to her ear and saying 'Hello?'. She just watched you. Much of what we learn, we learn by watching.
points: Observational learning (also called modelling or social learning): learning by observing the behaviour of others (models) and its consequences.
Bandura's Bobo doll experiment: children watched a film in which an adult hit and kicked an inflatable Bobo doll. In different versions, the model was rewarded, punished, or received no consequences.

Afterwards, children who saw the model punished showed the least aggression; but when all children were offered rewards to imitate, they all showed aggressive acts, proving that they had learned the behaviour by watching even if they had not performed it.
Observational learning explains socialisation (learning social norms and manners), fashion trends and many social skills, and also how violent media can teach aggression.

example.q: In Bandura's study, why did children who saw the model punished still hit the doll when offered rewards?
steps: Watching the model punished reduced their performance of aggression.
But they had still observed and learned the actions.
The reward gave them a reason to perform what they had learned.
example.answer: They had learned the behaviour through observation; punishment of the model only suppressed performance.

learn.reallife: Fashion and slang spread rapidly among Indian teens through Instagram reels and cricket stars' celebrations, which is observational learning on a national scale.

topics.title: Cognitive learning: insight and latent learning

learn.hook: You've been stuck on a geometry proof for twenty minutes, and then suddenly, 'Aha!' the whole solution clicks. That flash is the heart of cognitive learning.
points: Cognitive learning involves changes in what the learner knows (understanding, mental representations) rather than just in behaviour.

Insight learning (Wolfgang Kohler): chimpanzees (such as Sultan) placed in a cage with bananas out of reach first tried and failed, then paused and suddenly solved the problem, e.g. by joining two sticks or stacking boxes. Insight is sudden, and the solution is remembered and transferred to similar problems.

Latent learning (Edward Tolman): rats allowed to explore a maze without any reward later found the food quickly once a reward was introduced. They had formed a cognitive map (a mental representation of the layout), and learning stayed hidden (latent) until there was a reason to show it.
Insight vs latent: insight = sudden solution after a period of problem-solving; latent = learning without reinforcement that is not shown until needed.

example.q: Raghav cycles around his new neighbourhood with no particular goal. A month later, when a road is blocked, he immediately takes a detour he has never used. Which type of learning?
steps: He learned the layout without any reward → hidden learning.
It appeared only when there was a need.
He had formed a cognitive map → latent learning (Tolman).
example.answer: Latent learning (cognitive map)

learn.reallife: Delivery riders for Indian food apps who have explored a city for months build cognitive maps that let them find shortcuts instantly when a road is closed, a case of latent learning.

learn.hook: Memorising Hindi-English word pairs, the periodic table in order, or a shopping list in any order: each uses a different verbal-learning method that psychologists have studied since the 1880s.
points: Verbal learning: learning words and verbal material. Hermann Ebbinghaus pioneered it using nonsense syllables (e.g. consonant-vowel-consonant 'trigrams' like 'BEM', 'DIK') to avoid the influence of meaning.
Paired-associates learning: learning pairs, where the first word is the stimulus term and the second the response term, e.g. learning foreign-language words with their meanings.

Serial learning: learning items in a fixed order (e.g. planets from the Sun, steps of a procedure). Free recall: recalling items in any order; items at the beginning and end of a list are usually recalled better than those in the middle.

Determinants: length of list (longer → more trials needed), meaningfulness of material (meaningful material is learned faster), and how often items have been used (frequency). Organisation helps: clustering (recalling words in categories) and subjective organisation (the learner's own grouping of unrelated words).

example.q: Classify the method: (a) Learning 'chhatri - umbrella, kitaab - book'. (b) Learning the order of the planets. (c) Recalling 20 random words in any order you like.
steps: (a) Pairs with stimulus and response terms → paired-associates.
(b) Fixed order → serial learning.
(c) Any order → free recall.
example.answer: (a) paired-associates, (b) serial learning, (c) free recall

learn.reallife: Students preparing for UPSC learn lists of Articles of the Constitution as pairs (number - topic), a classic paired-associates task, and organise them into clusters like 'Fundamental Rights' to aid recall.

topics.title: Skill learning and factors that facilitate learning

learn.hook: Your first day of driving: mirror, clutch, gear, indicator, panic. A year later you drive while chatting about cricket. Skills go through predictable phases.
points: A skill is the ability to perform a complex task smoothly and efficiently; it involves a sequence of perceptual-motor responses (e.g. driving, typing, playing the tabla).

Fitts's three phases of skill learning: cognitive (understanding instructions, many errors, full attention), associative (errors reduce, steps get linked, performance improves) and autonomous (performance becomes automatic and needs little attention).
Practice, with feedback about performance, is essential for skill learning: skills improve with practice, and knowing results helps correct errors.
Motivation facilitates learning: intrinsic motivation (learning for its own sake, interest, enjoyment) and extrinsic motivation (learning for external rewards like marks or prizes).
Preparedness: species differ in their biological readiness to learn certain associations; some are learned very easily (e.g. linking taste with sickness), others with difficulty.

example.q: Identify the phase: (a) A new typist looks at the keys and makes many errors. (b) She types faster with fewer mistakes, though still with effort. (c) She types while talking, without looking.
steps: (a) Understanding and many errors → cognitive phase.
(b) Fewer errors, steps linked → associative phase.
(c) Automatic, little attention → autonomous phase.
example.answer: (a) cognitive, (b) associative, (c) autonomous

learn.reallife: Indian Air Force pilots move from classroom ground school (cognitive), through simulator hours (associative) to flying with automatic control habits (autonomous), with instructors giving constant feedback.

learn.hook: Taare Zameen Par made millions of Indians aware that a bright child who mixes up 'b' and 'd' is not lazy or stupid. He may have a learning disability, and with the right teaching he can thrive.
points: A learning disability is a general term for difficulties in acquiring and using reading, writing, speaking, listening, reasoning and mathematical skills, in people whose intelligence is normal. It is thought to arise from differences in how the brain processes information.

Common signs: difficulty in writing letters, words and phrases, in reading text aloud and in speaking; confusing similar letters (b/d, p/q) or reading 'was' as 'saw'; poor listening skills; attention problems; poor sense of time and space; poor motor coordination; poor learning strategies.

Dyslexia (difficulty in reading and spelling) is one of the most common forms. Learning disabilities are NOT due to intellectual disability, sensory impairment (e.g. poor eyesight) or lack of educational opportunity.
Early identification and remedial teaching (special methods suited to the child, often multi-sensory) help children with learning disabilities learn effectively; support at home and school matters.

example.q: Ishaan, aged 9, is good at drawing and solving puzzles but reverses letters while writing, struggles to read aloud and often loses track of time. His eyesight and hearing are normal. What might be the issue, and what should be done?
steps: Normal intelligence (good at puzzles) with specific difficulty in reading/writing.
Letter reversals, poor reading, poor time sense are signs of a learning disability.
Sensory problems are ruled out.
He should be assessed by a professional and given remedial teaching, with patient support.
example.answer: Possible learning disability (e.g. dyslexia); assessment and remedial teaching are needed.

learn.reallife: Under India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, specific learning disabilities are recognised, and CBSE allows support such as extra time or a scribe for eligible students in board exams.

topics.title: Nature of memory: encoding, storage and retrieval

learn.hook: You studied the Mughal timeline for an hour. In the exam hall, Akbar's dates refuse to come. Did you never store them, lose them, or just fail to find them? Memory can break at three different points.
points: Memory lets us retain information and use it over time: without it, we could not learn, recognise people or plan.
Memory is the process of retaining and recovering information over time.

Three stages: encoding (information is first recorded and registered in a usable form), storage (retaining the encoded information over time) and retrieval (bringing stored information back into awareness to use it).
Forgetting can result from a failure at any stage: poor encoding (never properly registered), poor storage (lost over time) or failed retrieval (stored but cannot be accessed).

example.q: Kabir meets a new classmate but is busy texting and never really notices her name. The next day he can't recall it. Which stage failed?
steps: He did not attend to or register the name.
So it was never properly recorded.
That is a failure of encoding.
example.answer: Encoding failure

learn.reallife: Like a bank locker system: you must deposit valuables properly (encoding), the vault must keep them safe (storage), and you need the right key to take them out (retrieval).

learn.hook: Your phone takes input from the camera, holds it in RAM while you edit, then saves it to storage. In 1968, two psychologists proposed that human memory works in a surprisingly similar way.
points: The information-processing approach uses a computer analogy: information is input, processed, stored and retrieved.
Atkinson and Shiffrin's stage model (1968) proposes three memory systems: sensory memory, short-term memory (STM) and long-term memory (LTM).
Control processes such as attention (moving information from sensory memory to STM) and rehearsal (keeping it in STM and helping transfer to LTM) move information between the stores.

Criticisms: the model treats STM as a passive store and memory as fixed boxes; later research showed STM is an active workspace (working memory) and that how deeply information is processed matters more than which box it is in, which led to alternative models.

example.q: Trace a phone number from hearing it to remembering it a year later in the stage model.
steps: Heard → briefly held in sensory memory.
Attended to → moves into STM.
Rehearsed and elaborated → transferred into LTM.
A year later → retrieved from LTM into STM to use.
example.answer: Sensory memory → (attention) → STM → (rehearsal) → LTM → retrieval

learn.reallife: Air India's cockpit checklists are designed knowing that pilots' STM is limited; critical steps are written down rather than relying on rehearsal alone.

learn.hook: Someone tells you an OTP, 739204, and you repeat it under your breath until you type it in. Ten seconds later, it's gone. That's short-term memory doing exactly what it is designed to do.
points: Sensory memory: large capacity but very brief duration (less than a second for visual images). Visual sensory memory is iconic memory; auditory sensory memory is echoic memory.
Short-term memory (STM): small capacity, about 7 ± 2 items (George Miller); duration about 30 seconds or less without rehearsal; information is encoded mainly acoustically (by sound).
Maintenance rehearsal (repeating information) keeps items in STM; chunking (grouping items into meaningful units, e.g. 9-8-7-6-5-4-3-2-1-0 as 98765 43210) increases how much STM can hold.

Forgetting from STM happens through decay and interference. In Peterson and Peterson's experiment, participants counted backwards (to prevent rehearsal) and recall of letter trios dropped sharply within about 18 seconds.
Maintenance rehearsal (rote repetition) only holds items in STM; elaborative rehearsal (linking new information with existing knowledge and meaning) helps transfer it to LTM.

example.q: Arrange 1-9-4-7-1-9-5-0-2-0-2-6 to make it easier to hold in STM.
steps: 12 separate digits exceed 7 ± 2.
Group them into meaningful chunks: 1947 (Independence), 1950 (Republic), 2026 (this year).
3 chunks fit easily in STM.

learn.reallife: Indian mobile numbers are often read as 98xxx xxxxx (two chunks of five) and Aadhaar as three blocks of four digits, so they fit STM limits.

learn.hook: Your grandmother remembers songs from her wedding 50 years ago but forgets where she kept her glasses five minutes ago. Long-term memory and working memory are very different systems.
points: Long-term memory (LTM): practically unlimited capacity, long duration (from minutes to a lifetime), and information encoded mainly semantically (by meaning).

Working memory (Baddeley): STM is not a passive store but an active workspace with three parts: the phonological loop (holds sounds/speech, e.g. repeating a number), the visuo-spatial sketchpad (holds visual and spatial information, e.g. picturing a route) and the central executive (directs attention and coordinates the other parts).
Comparison: sensory memory = large capacity, under a second; STM = 7 ± 2 items, about 30 seconds or less, acoustic; LTM = unlimited, long-lasting, semantic.
Working memory lets us do mental arithmetic, follow conversations and plan, by holding and manipulating information at the same time.

example.q: While calculating 23 × 4 in your head, you hold '23' and '4', compute 20 × 4 and 3 × 4, then combine. Which system is at work and which parts?
steps: You are holding and manipulating numbers at the same time → working memory.
Repeating numbers to yourself → phonological loop.
Planning the steps and switching between them → central executive.
example.answer: Working memory: phonological loop plus central executive

learn.hook: Ask yourself three questions about the word 'MANGO': Is it in capital letters? Does it rhyme with 'tango'? Is it a fruit? The question you answer changes how well you'll remember the word tomorrow.
points: Craik and Lockhart (1972) proposed that how well we remember depends on the depth (level) at which information is processed, not on which memory store it is in.
Structural (physical) processing: attending to physical features such as shape or case of letters; this is shallow processing with poor retention.
Phonetic (sound) processing: attending to how a word sounds, e.g. rhymes; intermediate level.
Semantic (meaning) processing: thinking about meaning and relating it to what we know; this is the deepest processing and gives the best retention.
Study tip: ask 'why' and 'how', make examples and connect ideas; this pushes processing to the semantic level.

example.q: For each question about the word 'DOCTOR', state the level: (a) Is it written in capitals? (b) Does it rhyme with 'proctor'? (c) Does it fit 'The ___ treated the patient'?
steps: (a) Physical appearance → structural (shallow).
(b) Sound → phonetic (intermediate).
(c) Meaning → semantic (deep).
Recall will be best for (c).
example.answer: (a) structural, (b) phonetic, (c) semantic; (c) is remembered best

learn.reallife: CBSE's push for competency-based questions rewards semantic processing: students who understand why a concept works remember it far better than those who just memorise how it looks.

learn.hook: You can easily tell a friend that Delhi is India's capital. Try telling her exactly how you balance on a bicycle. Some memories come with words; others live in your muscles.
points: Declarative (explicit) memory: memory for facts, names, dates and events that can be put into words and consciously recalled, e.g. 'Gandhiji was born in 1869'.
Procedural (non-declarative) memory: memory for how to do things, such as skills and habits (riding a cycle, tying shoelaces, typing); it is hard to put into words.

Implicit memory: memory that influences behaviour without conscious awareness or deliberate recall. Priming is an example: earlier exposure to a word makes it easier to recognise later, even if you don't remember seeing it.
Declarative memories are 'knowing that'; procedural memories are 'knowing how'.

example.q: Classify: (a) Remembering that water boils at 100 °C at sea level. (b) Knowing how to swim. (c) Choosing a brand you saw in an ad you don't remember noticing.
steps: (a) A fact you can state → declarative.
(b) A skill hard to describe → procedural.
(c) Influence without conscious recall → implicit memory (priming).
example.answer: (a) declarative, (b) procedural, (c) implicit

learn.hook: 'My first day in Class 11, when I sat next to Sneha and the fan broke' versus 'Photosynthesis needs sunlight.' Both live in declarative memory, but they are very different kinds.
points: Endel Tulving divided declarative memory into episodic and semantic memory.
Episodic memory: memory for personal life events and experiences, tied to a particular time and place (your last birthday party, your board exam day). It is often emotional.
Semantic memory: general knowledge about the world, concepts, word meanings, facts and rules (2 + 2 = 4, Delhi is the capital, grammar rules); it is not tied to when or where you learned it.
Exam tip: if the memory has a 'when and where I was', it is episodic; if it is general knowledge, it is semantic.

example.q: Classify: (a) Remembering what you ate at your cousin's wedding. (b) Knowing that the Himalayas are fold mountains. (c) Recalling the day India won the 2011 World Cup at your home.
steps: (a) Personal event with time and place → episodic.
(b) General fact → semantic.
(c) Personal experience with a specific time and place → episodic.
example.answer: (a) episodic, (b) semantic, (c) episodic

learn.reallife: A quiz-show contestant answering 'Who was India's first President?' uses semantic memory; talking about the excitement of being on the show uses episodic memory.

learn.hook: You learn French in Class 8, then switch to German in Class 9. Now when you try to say 'thank you' in French, German words keep popping up. Interference is at work.
points: Hermann Ebbinghaus studied forgetting with nonsense syllables and the savings method (how much less time it takes to relearn a list). His forgetting curve shows rapid forgetting soon after learning, after which the rate slows and levels off.

Trace decay (disuse) theory: memory traces fade with time if not used. Limitation: it can't explain why forgetting is greater when other activities fill the interval than when one sleeps, and why some old memories stay vivid.
Interference theory: forgetting happens because other learning competes with what we want to recall.
Proactive interference: earlier learning interferes with the recall of new learning (old blocks new).
Retroactive interference: new learning interferes with the recall of earlier learning (new blocks old).

example.q: (a) After changing your phone number, you keep giving your old number. (b) After learning your new number, you can't remember your old one. Identify the type of interference.
steps: (a) The old number blocks recall of the new one → proactive.
(b) The new number blocks recall of the old one → retroactive.
Remember: PRO = old works forward; RETRO = new works backward.
example.answer: (a) proactive, (b) retroactive

learn.reallife: Students who study History and then Political Science back-to-back on similar topics (constitutions, revolutions) often face interference; spacing similar subjects apart reduces it.

learn.hook: 'It's on the tip of my tongue!' You know the actor's name, you know it starts with 'R', but it just won't come. Then, at 2 a.m., it suddenly appears. The memory never left; you just lacked the key.
points: Retrieval failure (Tulving): forgetting occurs because the right retrieval cues are not available at the time of recall, even though the information is stored (cue-dependent forgetting).
Tip-of-the-tongue experiences show that information can be stored but temporarily inaccessible; partial cues (first letter, number of syllables) often help.
Memory is better when the cues present during recall match those present during learning (e.g. same place, same mood).
Motivated forgetting (repression), from Freud: memories that are painful or anxiety-provoking may be pushed out of conscious awareness.

example.q: Neha can't recall a classmate's name at a reunion, but when someone says 'She sat near the window in Class 6', the name comes instantly. Explain.
steps: The name was stored all along.
It was not accessible without a suitable cue.
The cue (the window seat) unlocked it → retrieval (cue-dependent) failure.
example.answer: Retrieval failure due to missing cues; the cue restored recall.

learn.reallife: Witnesses at police stations recall more details when taken back mentally to the scene (reinstating context cues), a technique used in cognitive interviews.

topics.title: Mnemonics using images: keyword method and method of loci

learn.hook: Ancient Greek orators memorised hours-long speeches by mentally walking through their homes and placing each idea in a room. You can use the same trick for your history answers.
points: Mnemonics are strategies that make information easier to remember, often by creating vivid images or organising material.

Keyword method (useful for foreign-language words): pick an English word that sounds like the foreign word (the keyword), then form an image linking the keyword with the foreign word's meaning. E.g. French 'pain' (bread): imagine a loaf of bread in pain, crying.

Method of loci: picture a familiar route or place (your house, your walk to school), and mentally 'place' each item to be remembered at a location along it; to recall, take the walk again in your mind.
Activity: test your digit span (how many digits you can repeat after hearing them once) and then try the method of loci with a 10-item list to see the improvement.

example.q: Use the method of loci to remember: notebook, eggs, battery, pen, umbrella.
steps: Choose a familiar route: gate → door → sofa → kitchen → bed.
Imagine a giant notebook blocking the gate, eggs smashing on the door, a battery sitting on the sofa, a pen stirring a pot in the kitchen, an umbrella open on the bed.
To recall, walk the route mentally and 'see' each item.
example.answer: Items placed along a familiar route and recalled by mentally walking it

learn.reallife: Memory-sport competitors use the method of loci to memorise long strings of digits and whole decks of cards; students can use it to remember sequences such as the order of the Mughal emperors.

topics.title: Mnemonics using organisation and general strategies

learn.hook: VIBGYOR has helped generations of Indian students remember the colours of the rainbow. Five letters of effort, a lifetime of recall.
points: Chunking: grouping items into larger meaningful units (e.g. 1-9-4-7 as '1947'), which lets STM hold more.
First-letter technique: take the first letter of each item and form a word or sentence (acronym/acrostic), e.g. VIBGYOR for violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red.

General strategies: engage in deep (semantic) processing; minimise interference (avoid studying similar material back-to-back, take breaks, sleep); give yourself retrieval cues (organise notes with headings, link to context).
PQRST method: Preview the chapter, form Questions, Read to answer them, Self-recite (say the answers in your own words), and Test yourself.
Spreading study over time and testing yourself work better than last-minute cramming.

example.q: Create a first-letter mnemonic for the four goals of psychological enquiry: description, prediction, explanation, control.
steps: First letters: D, P, E, C.
Make a memorable phrase: 'Dogs Play Every Cricket match'.
Recall the phrase → letters → goals.
example.answer: 'Dogs Play Every Cricket match' → Description, Prediction, Explanation, Control

learn.hook: Deciding which coaching class to join, planning a route when the metro is shut, figuring out why your plant is wilting: a large part of your day is thinking, even when you don't call it that.
points: Thinking is the base of all cognitive activities such as problem solving, reasoning, decision making and creativity.
Thinking is a higher mental process through which we manipulate and analyse acquired or existing information; it is mainly goal-directed and organised.
Thinking is an internal mental process that cannot be observed directly; it is inferred from overt behaviour (what a person says or does, e.g. the solution produced).
As a process, thinking involves understanding information, organising it, and using it to reach a goal, often by working with mental representations rather than real objects.

example.q: A chess player sits still for five minutes, then makes a brilliant move. How do we know she was thinking?
steps: Her thinking itself was not visible.
Her move (overt behaviour) shows the result of mental manipulation of possibilities.
So her thinking is inferred from her behaviour.
example.answer: Thinking is inferred from her overt behaviour (the move she made).

learn.reallife: ISRO mission planners simulate launch windows and trajectories mentally and on computers before anything is built: thinking with representations instead of real rockets.

topics.title: Building blocks of thought: mental images and concepts

learn.hook: Close your eyes and picture your school gate. Now think of 'fruit'. In one case you 'saw' something; in the other you used a category. Those are the two building blocks of thought.
points: Mental images are mental representations of sensory experiences: we can 'see' a place, 'hear' a song or 'smell' a dish in the mind's eye without the stimulus being present.
Concepts are mental categories for objects, events, ideas or people that share common features, e.g. 'fruit', 'vehicle', 'democracy'. They help us organise knowledge and think efficiently.
Concept formation: we learn which features belong to a category; a prototype is the most typical example of a concept (a mango or apple is a more typical 'fruit' for an Indian child than a tomato).
Concepts are arranged in hierarchies, e.g. 'furniture' (broad) → 'chair' (basic) → 'office chair' (specific).

example.q: Explain how you use mental images and concepts to give directions to your house.
steps: Mental image: you picture the route, the turn after the temple, the blue gate.
Concepts: you use categories like 'traffic signal', 'second lane', 'opposite the park'.
Both together let you think and describe the route without being there.
example.answer: Mental images let you 'see' the route; concepts let you categorise and describe landmarks.

learn.reallife: Architects designing metro stations picture the space (mental images) and use concepts like 'entry', 'platform' and 'emergency exit' to plan layouts.

learn.hook: Your bicycle chain slips just before a tuition class across town. You have 20 minutes, ₹50 and a phone. Welcome to problem solving: getting from where you are to where you want to be.
points: Problem solving is thinking directed towards reaching a goal: moving from an initial state (the problem) to a goal state (the solution) when the path is not obvious.
Step 1, identify the problem: understand what exactly is wrong and what the goal is.
Step 2, represent the problem: describe it in a useful form, e.g. a diagram, list or equation.
Step 3, plan and generate possible solutions; Step 4, evaluate the solutions (try them, check results) and choose the best one; if it fails, go back and re-represent the problem.

example.q: Use the problem-solving steps for: 'My exam is in 10 days and I have 6 chapters left.'
steps: Identify: 6 chapters to finish and revise in 10 days.
Represent: draw a 10-day timetable with chapters and difficulty.
Plan solutions: 1 chapter per day for 6 days + 4 days revision; or 2 hard chapters over 3 days each.
Evaluate: pick the plan that leaves time for revision; adjust after day 3 if behind.
example.answer: Identify → represent (timetable) → plan options → evaluate and choose (e.g. 6 days of chapters + 4 days revision).

learn.reallife: When Kerala's 2018 floods cut roads, relief teams identified isolated areas, mapped them, planned boat and helicopter routes and evaluated which worked fastest: systematic problem solving under pressure.

topics.title: Obstacles to problem solving: mental set, functional fixedness, motivation

learn.hook: Given a candle, a box of drawing pins and matches, can you fix the candle to the wall? Most people try pinning the candle directly. Few think of emptying the box and pinning it as a shelf. Why?
points: Mental set: a tendency to solve problems using a strategy that worked before, even when a simpler or better method exists. It helps with routine problems but blocks new solutions.
Functional fixedness: seeing objects only in terms of their usual function (a pin box is for holding pins, not a shelf), which prevents creative uses.
Lack of motivation or persistence: giving up too early, or not being interested enough, can stop people from reaching solutions even when they have the ability.
Overcoming obstacles: step back, re-represent the problem, ask 'what else could this object do?', take a break, and stay motivated.

example.q: Raj solves ten maths problems using a long formula. The eleventh can be solved by a simple shortcut, but he uses the long formula again and gets stuck. Which obstacle?
steps: He keeps using a strategy that worked before.
This blinds him to a simpler method.
That is mental set.
example.answer: Mental set

learn.reallife: The famous 'jugaad' of using a pressure cooker as a steam iron or a bottle as a lamp shows Indians overcoming functional fixedness every day.

learn.hook: Sherlock Holmes reasons from clues to the culprit; a scientist reasons from many observations to a law; a lawyer reasons from past cases to a new one. Same skill, three different directions.
points: Reasoning is the process of gathering and analysing information to arrive at conclusions; it is goal-directed and logical.

Deductive reasoning: from a general premise (assumption) to a specific conclusion. E.g. 'All mammals breathe air; a dolphin is a mammal; so a dolphin breathes air.' If a premise is false, the conclusion can be wrong even if the logic is valid.
Inductive reasoning: from specific facts or observations to a general conclusion. E.g. 'Every metal I have heated has expanded; so metals expand on heating.' Conclusions are probable, not certain.
Analogical reasoning: solving a new problem by transferring the solution from a similar, familiar problem (e.g. understanding electric current by comparing it to water flowing in pipes).
Common error in deduction: starting from a wrong general belief, e.g. 'All people from a city are rude', leads to unfair conclusions about individuals.

example.q: Classify: (a) 'Every time it rained this week, the train was late, so rain always delays trains.' (b) 'All students must wear ID cards; Arjun is a student; so Arjun must wear an ID card.'
steps: (a) From specific observations to a general rule → inductive.
(b) From a general rule to a specific case → deductive.
example.answer: (a) inductive, (b) deductive

learn.reallife: Doctors use deduction ('all patients with these symptoms need test X; this patient has them') and induction (noticing a pattern across many patients that suggests a new disease outbreak).

learn.hook: Science or Arts? Hostel or home? Delhi University or a college near home? Class 11 is full of decisions, and psychology shows they are rarely made by cold logic alone.
points: Judgement: drawing conclusions, forming opinions and evaluating objects, events or people on the basis of available information (e.g. judging that a teacher is strict).
Decision-making: choosing among two or more alternatives; it relies on judgements about each option. Judgement and decision-making are closely interrelated.
Factors in decisions: personal values, costs and benefits of each option, risk involved, emotions at the time, and past experience.
Heuristics are mental shortcuts or rules of thumb that allow quick decisions but can lead to errors (e.g. choosing a product because it is the one you remember seeing most).

example.q: Meera must choose between two colleges. Show how judgement and decision-making work together.
steps: Judgements: College A has better faculty; College B is closer and cheaper.
Weigh values and costs: she values quality but her family has a tight budget.
Consider risk and emotions: moving away feels exciting but stressful.
Decision: she chooses the option that best fits her values and constraints.
example.answer: She judges each option, then weighs values, costs, risk and emotions to decide.

learn.reallife: Investors on Indian stock markets often follow 'hot tips' (a heuristic) instead of analysing company data, which shows how shortcuts and emotions shape financial decisions.

topics.title: Creative thinking: nature, features, convergent and divergent thinking

learn.hook: How many uses can you think of for an old newspaper in two minutes? Wrapping, a fan, a hat, a paper boat, a mat at a picnic... The more and the stranger the ideas, the more creative the thinking.
points: Creative thinking produces ideas or products that are both novel (new, original) and appropriate (useful, fitting the situation).

Features of creative (divergent) thinking: fluency (number of ideas), flexibility (variety of different kinds of ideas, shifting categories), originality (unusual, rare ideas) and elaboration (developing and adding detail to ideas).
Convergent thinking aims at one correct answer (e.g. solving 8 × 7); divergent thinking generates many possible answers (e.g. uses for a brick).
Activity: list unusual uses of an everyday object to practise divergent thinking; count your ideas (fluency), categories (flexibility) and rare ideas (originality).

example.q: Priya lists uses for a bucket: carry water, store rice, a drum, a stool, a plant pot, a hat for a scarecrow. How would you score her fluency and flexibility?
steps: Count ideas: 6 → fluency = 6.
Group by category: container uses (water, rice, plant pot), music (drum), furniture (stool), clothing/costume (hat).
4 categories → flexibility = 4.
example.answer: Fluency = 6 ideas, flexibility = 4 categories

learn.reallife: Indian startups like those born in college incubators often begin with divergent brainstorming of many ideas, then use convergent thinking to choose the one that works.

topics.title: Stages of creative thinking, strategies and barriers

learn.hook: As the famous story goes, Archimedes struggled for days with how to measure the gold in a crown. The answer came when he stepped into a bath and saw the water rise: 'Eureka!' That flash came only after hard preparation and a break.
points: Stages of creative thinking: preparation (understanding the problem, gathering information), incubation (a period of not consciously working on it; ideas mature in the background), illumination (the sudden 'aha' insight) and verification (testing and evaluating the solution).
Strategies: become aware of your habitual ways of thinking, generate many ideas (brainstorming), defer judgement (don't criticise ideas too early), and allow time for incubation.

Barriers to creative thinking: habitual (relying on habits), perceptual (seeing things only one way), motivational (lack of interest or fear of failure), emotional (anxiety, fear of being judged) and cultural (pressure to conform, fear of being different).
Exam tip: arrange the creative stages correctly, then describe one example for each.

example.q: A student is designing a poster for a road-safety competition. Show the four stages.
steps: Preparation: collects facts on accidents and looks at sample posters.
Incubation: leaves the task for two days and does other work.
Illumination: suddenly thinks of showing a helmet as a 'shield' in a superhero style.
Verification: sketches it, tests it on friends and refines it.
example.answer: Preparation → incubation → illumination → verification

learn.reallife: Many breakthroughs at Indian research labs come after scientists step away from a problem; teams now build in breaks and brainstorming sessions to support incubation.

topics.title: Thought and language: Whorf, Piaget and Vygotsky

learn.hook: Hindi has separate words for your father's elder brother (taaya) and younger brother (chacha); English lumps them into 'uncle'. Does having more words change how you think about family?
points: Language determines thought: Benjamin Lee Whorf's linguistic relativity hypothesis says that the language we speak shapes (and in its strong form, determines) how we think and perceive the world.
Thought determines language: Jean Piaget held that thought comes first; language develops from thought and reflects the child's level of cognitive development.
Different origins: Lev Vygotsky argued that thought and language develop separately until about age two, after which they merge: thought becomes verbal and speech becomes rational.
Current view: thought and language influence each other; language can make some distinctions easier to notice, but does not completely fix what we can think.

example.q: Which view fits each statement? (a) 'Because Hindi has words for many kinds of relatives, Hindi speakers notice those relationships more.' (b) 'A child can use the word bigger only after understanding size comparison.' (c) 'Before age two, a baby thinks without words and babbles without thought; then the two join.'
steps: (a) Language shaping thought → Whorf.
(b) Thought must come first → Piaget.
(c) Separate development, then merging → Vygotsky.
example.answer: (a) Whorf, (b) Piaget, (c) Vygotsky

learn.reallife: India's multilingual classrooms, where students switch between Hindi, English and a regional language, offer researchers natural tests of how language and thought interact.

topics.title: Language: components and stages of development

learn.hook: A toddler says 'Mummy goed market.' It's wrong, but brilliant: she has figured out that '-ed' makes the past tense and applied the rule everywhere. Language develops by rules, not just copying.
points: Language is a system of symbols (sounds, words, signs) organised by rules, used to communicate and to think.

Components: phonemes (smallest units of sound, e.g. /k/ in 'kitab'), morphemes (smallest units of meaning, e.g. 'un-', 'happy', '-ness' in 'unhappiness'), syntax (rules for combining words into sentences) and semantics (meaning of words and sentences).

Stages: crying (from birth) → cooing (vowel-like 'oo', 'aa' sounds in the first months) → babbling (consonant-vowel strings like 'ba-ba-ba', around 6 months) → one-word stage (around one year; a single word can express a whole idea, a holophrase, e.g. 'milk!' = 'I want milk').

Then the two-word stage and telegraphic speech (short sentences with only key words, 'Daddy go office'), followed by more complex sentences; overgeneralisation (applying a rule too widely, e.g. 'goed', 'mouses') shows that children learn rules.

example.q: Identify the stage or term: (a) A 6-month-old says 'da-da-da-da'. (b) A 13-month-old says 'Ball!' meaning 'Give me the ball'. (c) A 2-year-old says 'Want juice'. (d) A 3-year-old says 'I runned fast'.
steps: (a) Consonant-vowel repetition → babbling.
(b) One word for a whole idea → holophrase (one-word stage).
(c) Key words only → telegraphic speech.
(d) Past-tense rule over-applied → overgeneralisation.
example.answer: (a) babbling, (b) holophrase, (c) telegraphic speech, (d) overgeneralisation

topics.title: Theories of language acquisition and bilingualism

learn.hook: Children everywhere, whether in Chennai, Kolkata or Tokyo, pick up the grammar of their language in a few years, without formal lessons. Is that because they are rewarded, or because they are born ready?
points: B.F. Skinner's learning view: children learn language through imitation of adults and reinforcement (praise or getting what they want when they speak correctly), and through shaping of babbling into words.

Noam Chomsky's view: children are born with an innate language acquisition device (LAD) that contains a universal grammar; exposure to any language activates it, which explains rapid learning and errors like 'goed' that were never imitated.
Criticism of each: Skinner's view cannot easily explain novel sentences and overgeneralisation errors; Chomsky's view gives less weight to the role of the social environment.

Bilingualism (using two languages) and multilingualism are common in India; bilingual children can switch between languages and often show cognitive flexibility. Language use also reflects culture and social relationships.

example.q: A child says 'I goed to school.' Which theory explains this better, Skinner's or Chomsky's?
steps: No adult says 'goed', so it isn't imitation.
It's not reinforced either.
The child is applying an internal rule (add -ed), supporting an innate rule-learning capacity → Chomsky.
example.answer: Chomsky's LAD (innate rule learning) explains it better.

topics.title: Nature of motivation: motive, need, drive and incentive

learn.hook: Why does one student practise cricket at 5 a.m. in winter while another can't get out of bed for an exam? Same body, same alarm clock. The difference is motivation.
points: Motivation and emotion are forces that start, energise and guide behaviour.
The word 'motive' comes from the Latin 'movere', meaning 'to move'. A motive is a general state that energises behaviour and directs it towards a goal.

Need: a lack or deficit of something (e.g. water, food, affection). Drive: the state of tension or arousal produced by a need, which pushes us to act. Incentive: an external object or condition that attracts us and can motivate behaviour (e.g. a prize, tasty food).
Motives cannot be seen directly; they are inferred from behaviour, especially its direction (selectivity: choosing some goals over others) and persistence (continuing until the goal is reached).

example.q: After a long cricket match, Rohan is thirsty, feels restless and heads to a juice stall that advertises 'free lassi with every sandwich'. Identify need, drive and incentive.
steps: Lack of water in the body → need.
Restless urge to drink → drive.
Attractive free lassi offer → incentive.
example.answer: Need = water deficit; drive = urge/tension to drink; incentive = free lassi offer

learn.reallife: Salary hikes, Diwali bonuses and 'employee of the month' awards are incentives Indian companies use to direct employees' behaviour.

learn.hook: Thirsty → restless → walk to the water cooler → drink → relief. Then a few hours later, the whole loop starts again. Motivation runs in cycles.
points: Motivational cycle: need → drive → goal-directed behaviour (instrumental response) → goal attainment → need reduction (relief). Then a new need may arise.
Example: lack of food (need) → hunger drive → looking for food → eating (goal attained) → hunger reduced.
Biological (physiological) motives arise from bodily needs: hunger, thirst, sleep, temperature regulation.
Homeostasis: the body's tendency to maintain a stable internal state (e.g. body temperature, water and sugar levels). Imbalance creates needs and drives; satisfying them restores balance.

example.q: Describe the motivational cycle for a student who feels sleepy at 11 p.m.
steps: Need: body requires rest after a long day.
Drive: drowsiness and urge to sleep.
Goal-directed behaviour: switches off the light, goes to bed.
Goal attainment: sleeps.
Need reduction: wakes up refreshed.
example.answer: Need for rest → drowsiness drive → going to bed → sleep → refreshed (need reduced)

learn.reallife: During peak summer in Rajasthan, the body's homeostatic thirst drive rises sharply, which is why public water huts (pyaus) along roads are a long-standing tradition.

learn.hook: Ever felt 'hungry' the moment the aroma of samosas drifted from a stall, though you had just eaten? Hunger isn't only about an empty stomach.
points: Internal signals of hunger: stomach contractions (pangs), low blood-sugar (glucose) levels, and signals from the liver about the body's nutrient (energy) levels.

The hypothalamus regulates eating: the lateral hypothalamus (LH) acts as a feeding (excitatory) centre, and the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) acts as a satiety (inhibitory) centre that signals 'stop eating'.
External cues also trigger hunger: the sight, smell and taste of food, meal times and social situations (eating more at parties).
Thirst: signals include dryness of the mouth and throat and loss of water from body cells (dehydration); the hypothalamus detects the water imbalance and triggers the drive to drink.

example.q: Explain why you may still eat dessert at a wedding after a full meal.
steps: Internal signals (stomach full, VMH satiety) say stop.
But external cues (sight and smell of gulab jamun, social setting) are strong.
External cues can override internal satiety signals.
example.answer: External cues such as sight, smell and social setting can trigger eating despite internal satiety.

learn.reallife: On long summer train journeys, the dry heat causes water loss from cells, so passengers feel intense thirst and vendors selling chilled water do brisk business at every station.
